https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y: John Motson was a legendary football commentator who covered 10 World Cups, 10 European Championships and 29 FA Cup finals for BBC Sport
Football game EA Sports FC will feature the digitally recreated voice of the late commentator John Motson, Electronic Arts has exclusively told the BBC.
Motson, who died in 2023, was the main commentator for BBC Sport for decades - and performed the same role for the video game series during the 90s and 00s.
It is the first time the hit series, formerly known as Fifa, has featured a deceased commentator.
With the permission of his widow and his son, Motson's voice has been synthesised using a combination of old recording sessions and generative AI. It will become available in FC 27 on 26 November.
The legendary commentator died aged 77 in February 2023 - several months after the launch of ChatGPT and the massive growth of AI it set in train.
Fred Motson told the BBC it "means an awful lot" to have his dad's voice in EA Sports FC once again.
"I grew up with Fifa," he said. "I always used to tell my parents that I needed the latest console for Christmas because otherwise dad couldn't see how the game worked."

Electronic Arts, which was bought for $55bn (£42bn) in August , told the BBC it paid Motson's family for the rights to use his likeness and recreate his voice, but would not disclose the financial terms of the deal.
The BBC's lead football commentator Guy Mowbray said it was a "privilege" to be involved in the game, which he has provided commentary for since 2023.
"I think it's quite a nice, sort of non-scary use of AI," he said.
"We're in the business of nostalgia... I hear commentary not in my own voice, but in John's voice, because that's the voice I knew growing up.
"So I think it's nice that that legacy can be continued in this way."
WATCH: The new John Motson commentary in EA Sports FC 27 - and how it sounded back in Fifa 1998
John Motson was the first commentator for the series, appearing on games from Fifa 96 up to Fifa 2005. He later made a brief cameo in Fifa 19.
"While he completely understood when they went in a different direction, I think he really missed it after he left the game and it felt like a bit of an end of an era," his son said.
EA told the BBC the studio would not have included Motson in the game unless they had permission from his family.
"There was no way we would have moved forward with this in any way, shape or form if they weren't fully on board," said Mat Prior, senior game design director at EA Sports FC.

"At the outset we wanted to pay tribute to to Motty as the commentator and as this emotional connection - he was the very first voice of our game - so we really wanted to do him justice and bring him back."

He explained that Motson's voice in the game was a combination of old lines he recorded over the years and AI - tech which he said was "the only way" to make it happen, as they don't have recordings of him talking about modern players like Bradley Barcola and Chloe Kelly.
Gazza's tears, Radford's screamer & the Crazy Gang - 5 of Motty's best
Motson's son Fred said he believed his dad would have "absolutely" wanted to be involved in the game after his death.
"My dad was the least technological person in the world," he said. "Till his dying day, he had a typewriter on his desk.
"So I don't think he would have quite understood what the AI was doing technologically - but I think, on the other hand, he was always really keen to get involved in these kinds of projects."
But Peter Caulfield, founder of Save Our Voices Now which campaigns against AI voice cloning, expressed some disquiet about the project, and the fact Motson had been unable to consent to it.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crpd: US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about US President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday whether the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged spy who previously ran Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.
Trump has said he would consider pardoning Huang for any potential criminal activity, though he does not think it will come to that.
"It's always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary," Trump told the New York Post in an interview published on Tuesday.
With Huang rescue, Trump riskily ties his political fortunes to Nvidia
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.
The commerce and justice departments said last week that they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" .
But Blanche told reporters on Tuesday that the latter had "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.

Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with inquiries into whether it or Huang knew about chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.

"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.

Huang reportedly apologised to Nvidia employees on Tuesday, the day after returning to the company as chief executive, saying he had made "terrible mistakes" and was now receiving daily 90-minute therapy sessions.
The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, its chairman, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
On Monday, Trump said he had spoken to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang .
Republican Congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".
Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".

Democratic Congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy: Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable. Futurist or like-a-toaster depending on your point of view. But it's changed her life.
"I got it because I really needed it to get to school. And I use it to visit friends on the weekends. It's indispensable in rural areas like where I live," she says.
In France, you can drive a car like this from the age of 14 with a road safety certificate and eight hours training. In Italy too.
In Germany and Spain it's 15, in the UK 16 , external . Because they are classed as motorised quadri-cycles. Four-wheel mopeds in other words.
Registrations have risen from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year in France.

In Europe, sales have gone from 30,000 to 60,000 in the past five years. And the Ami, launched in 2020, has really changed the image, with teenagers who now account for a quarter of all mini-car sales.
In Selena's very small Citroën, we are soon rolling along at the top speed of 45km/h (28mph). For other road users, no-licence cars like this can seem like mobile traffic calming.
"When I'm on faster roads and there's a lot of traffic the cars behind me sometimes honk their horns but I can't go any quicker!" Selena says.
Daniel Laprès says the Aixam car was "the exact solution to our problem"
Another local Daniel Laprès, who drives a micro-car made by French firm and market-leader Aixam, tells me he actually pulls over to let the cars behind pass.

He and his wife moved from Paris to this country village two years ago. Of Canadian nationality, he didn't swap his foreign licence for a French one in time and lost the right to drive. That didn't matter much when he was in Paris. Like many Parisians he didn't need a car. He used public transport. But that's not possible here.

"We tried living off of taxis and it was in the end a disaster. Then we heard about how you could drive without having to have a licence, and it was the exact solution to our problem. Cheap, inexpensive to operate, basically no administrative formalities, you get insurance."
However, Laprès feels less safe in his small car. "They're little more than tin cans on wheels, right? I mean, you're not going to be driving fast, but someone else could be."
These cars are forbidden on motorways. But even on medium-fast roads, being considerably slower than the average vehicle can be a problem.

"You go on national highways at your risk and peril. I did it once and I will never, ever do it again. On those roads (speed limit 110km/h), everybody is passing you, including the biggest trucks. And they come at you very fast from the rear, so it's scary," Laprès says.
Daniel is 77 so fits in with the long-established market for these cars: older people living in the countryside.

Traditionally the market also included quite a few people who'd lost their licences, often because of drink-driving offences. But the launch of the electric Citroën Ami in 2020 changed the customer profile and the product.

"The launch of the Ami was the beginning of the transformation of the sector, with more and more electric models coming on to the market. In 2026, more than 67% of new licence-free cars are electric," says Marie-Laure Nivot, market analyst at AAA Data.
The launch of the Citroën Ami in 2020 "transformed the sector" analysts say
This tendency was encouraged by stricter EU regulations on motorised two-wheelers that had been the vehicles of choice for European teenagers until then.

"It proved too costly for manufacturers to apply the new EU rules, so mopeds and small scooters have almost disappeared from the market since 2020 and licence-free cars have taken their place," Marie-Laure Nivot says.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9gk: I've just spent a week using Muse, Meta's AI agent that rolls out in the UK today.
Agents are systems that don't just respond to questions but can carry out tasks for you. With Muse, Meta gives the examples of "searching for a cheaper energy deal" or "sorting the school calendar."
And it's true that it has helped me run my life - but it also challenged my personal privacy boundaries, and made me endure some cringeworthy interactions.
It has made a truly enormous bet on AI - of the $145bn (£111bn) it will spend this year much of it will be on building out the tech.

For that to pay off we all need to start using it much more, and Meta hopes Muse will do for AI agents what WhatsApp did for messaging - that is, become the AI agent of choice for billions of people, putting Meta at the forefront of the AI revolution.
But it's not just about what consumers think. Regulators are keeping a careful eye on these emerging tools too.
"Agentic AI has significant potential to benefit people and businesses", the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) noted as Muse launched in the UK.

But its chief executive, Paul Arnold, added it had been "clear with Meta about its responsibilities under data protection law prior to launch, particularly the requirement to ensure that users and the wider public can meaningfully understand and control how their personal data is used in the Muse product".
Muse bills itself as a personal AI agent available to anyone aged 18 and over.
"It doesn't just answer questions, it actually goes out and does work for you," said David Singleton, Meta's VP of engineering on AI products.
"So it helps people stay on top of things," he added. "[It] helps you take tasks and projects off your plate, and also helps you turn your long-term goals into action plans."

What this means is you can set it up to do something for you, like find some specific holiday options, and it will work away on that even as you move off the app and get on with your day, reporting back once it has finished.
It won't book the holiday without your permission - but it can then make the purchase, if you let it.
And the permission requests keep on coming. Every time Muse wants to do something, send something or post something, you have to allow it.

It is reassuring to know that an AI agent isn't running amok in your name, even if it also gets a bit annoying, though you can give it more autonomy (and so get fewer messages) if you adjust the settings.
Muse can't access many apps at the moment but the fundamental ones are the most personal.
I found myself wincing as I hooked it up to one of my personal email accounts, my personal calendar and my personal phone messages. I did not allow it any access to my BBC accounts.
It can't access WhatsApp except to set up a separate chat between it and the user, and while it found me some train tickets, it could not book them via the app which I use, and which is cheaper.

Amazon has blocked it from its marketplace, citing data security concerns but my agent didn't seem to know that, and spent a fruitless hour repeatedly telling me it was still waiting for the page to load in order to find me some shelves.
A number of big UK firms are working with Meta though, including Marks & Spencer, Debenhams Group, Currys, Sainsbury's and Ocado.
The ICO is urging consumers to be cautious with AI agents though: "consider the pros and cons," it said in a blog post to coincide with Muse's launch. , external
"Agents can make mistakes. Mistakes can be magnified if the agent is acting autonomously," it noted.
Meta is keen to emphasise how its agents can be personalised: "No two Muses are alike," , external it says in its press release.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv98: The US has said it intends to ban a Singaporean artificial intelligence (AI) company allegedly tied to the Nvidia scandal from doing business in America.
The Department of Commerce announced it planned to add Megaspeed Ltd to a list of entities that are blacklisted from buying or selling goods in the US.

The company is mainly a developer of data centres, but in recent weeks a former executive of Megaspeed was accused of working as a spy for China while having a romantic relationship with Nvidia head Jensen Huang.
The relationship led to additional scrutiny by US officials and heightened concern that Megaspeed was funnelling Nvidia's advanced AI computer chips to China.

When exactly the ban against Megaspeed will go into effect was not specified in the commerce department announcement. The BBC has asked the agency for comment, along with the White House and Megaspeed.
Megaspeed was not well known within the US until last month when media reports emerged that a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, had an affair with Jensen Huang.
Alice Huang (no relation) was thought by US intelligence to be working as an asset for Beijing, creating national security concerns within the US.
China has denied that she is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.
On 12 November, Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had had another affair, this one with a Nvidia employee.
On Monday, Nvidia's board reinstated him after US President Donald Trump said he had "convinced" the company and "made the deal".
The commerce department has said it had been investigating Megaspeed for almost two years.
The department said it had suspected the company was violating US export controls by helping to get Nvidia's chips into the hands of companies within China.
China has been blocked from buying such technology since 2022.
Although based in Singapore, Megaspeed has significant business dealings in China.
Alibaba, for instance, the major Chinese online retailer, has been reported to be one if its largest customers.
Megaspeed was a known buyer of billions of dollars of Nvidia computer chips, including through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, which has also been added to the Commerce blacklist.
Nvidia's computer chips, originally designed for use in gaming consols, in recent years have become crucial to the continued growth of the AI industry.

Without enough supply or access to computer chips that are capable of processing the huge amount of data needed to make things like AI chatbots and models run, AI companies will not be able to meet or grow demand from people using AI tools.
That has driven up the value of Nvidia on the stock market, as well as its influence in the AI industry and the White House.
Although tech stocks have in recent months been volatile and trending lower, when Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia because of his affairs, the company's stock fell by more than 30%.
Anxiety about the company's influence and ability to operate within the AI ecosystem without its famed executive appeared to take down shares of other tech companies, too.
Huang was reinstated on Monday to his position as head of Nvidia, a move that US President Donald Trump said he told the company's board to take .
The company's stock rallied on his reinstatement, as did several other tech stocks, but shares of Nvidia did not climb to where the company had been before being immersed in scandal.
In the weeks ahead, Huang and the company he now runs again are facing multiple government agency investigations.
Huang and the chief legal officer of Nvidia are set to appear next for a closed-door briefing with the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq62: A comeback for the ages: Trump's influence on Huang's return to Nvidia
Nvidia's market value rose by nearly $1 trillion as its share price skyrocketed after the tech firm reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive with immediate effect.

His shock reinstatement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy, a period in which shares in the chipmaker have also fallen significantly.
Nvidia shares rose by more than 31% which also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq climbing by 6.5% and the S&P 500 also rose 4.75%.
Tech stocks more broadly have also rallied following large falls on Friday , with much of the rally starting in pre-market trading before Huang's return was announced.
Other chipmakers experienced large increases following Monday's announcement from the Nvidia board. Shares in Micron Technology jumped 19%, while AMD shares rose nearly 7%.
Tesla shares also lept up by nearly 11.5%, while other tech gains were more muted by comparison: Amazon shares were up nearly 3.5%, and Apple and Microsoft rose by less than 2%.
While the surge in Nvidia shares was large and drove its market value back towards $4tn, the firm's share price remains about 21% down from a month ago.
A sharp drop occurred on 4 November, after the Democrat's midterm election victory sparked fears of tougher AI regulation to come led to a broad tech stock sell-off.

On Friday alone, Nvidia shares fell by 13.7% as tech stocks more broadly fell, and as Reuters reported - unconfirmed by the BBC - that the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) over its accounting practices.
Nvidia is a key firm at the core of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with the chips it makes central to the industry.

Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate the firm's co-founder following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him, the company said - but US President Donald Trump has claimed he "convinced" the board to reinstate Huang.
Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage firm XTB, said Huang's return showed Huang was the "godfather" of AI, and "has a talismanic influence over the sector".
"Barely two weeks ago this man was ousted from the company that he founded due to serious misconduct and potential national security issues," she said.
"Even though Huang did not hold special voting shares on the board, Nvidia's directors cannot see a future for the company without him."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said Huang's reinstatement was an astonishing about-turn for Nvidia, particularly given reports of an as-yet unconfirmed SEC investigation.

"This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world's most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable," he said.
"Today's stock market rebound represents a massive sigh of relief by investors. However, one cannot rule out a more conservative approach by Huang going forward.
"His every move will be scrutinised by the market, and he may wish to tread more carefully to protect his integrity and ensure that Nvidia is being run responsibly."

Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said Huang's reinstatement "reportedly at the encouragement of Trump Administration officials and without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation."
She added: "What is abundantly clear is that the AI industry requires guardrails and oversight."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c687: Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.
That central position prompted questions, in the aftermath of Huang's departure over revelations of extramarital affairs, over how important he was to the wider AI industry and US economy.
The fact he has been handed his job back after just 11 days in a U-turn by Nvidia's board implies the top brass believe Huang is irreplaceable.
Shares in the company have surged on the news of Huang's shock return, following a period of sharp declines.
While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.
The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.
Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.
It is now one the most valuable firms in the world and its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.
Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on it, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.
Some suggested his departure, which was sparked by the emergence that Huang had an affair with a woman alleged to have been a spy for China, posed a risk to the wider AI industry.

That was because it was unclear whether Nvidia would change strategy and potentially rein in spending - a move could have had wider implications for the US economy, but which looks unlikely now Huang has returned.

The fears were sparked due to Nvidia being a key source of finance for many firms, as well as being a microchip supplier. On its journey to the top of the AI industry, it has, through Huang, created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".

Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.

The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?
That risk was perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, had called for Huang's reinstatement.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, and backed a campaign, along with shareholders and supporters, to "Bring Jensen Back".
Following the announcement of Huang's return, Musk posted: "The mistake has been corrected."
Kathleen Brooks, research director at investment platform XTB, said Huang's return suggested he was "the godfather" of AI and has the status to shift "the dial for corporate finance".

"Is Jensen Huang the most valuable man on the planet? His return suggests more of the same when it comes to circular financing and the rapid AI infrastructure build out, and the market loves it," she added.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmze: For a long time it seemed that Jensen Huang, the leather jacket-clad founder of Nvidia, dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", could do no wrong.
Then came allegations of two affairs - one with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy - that rocked the world of tech and the global stock market. Huang resigned.
Now, just 11 days later, he's been reinstated by the board, who says it believes he is the right person to lead the company.
So what do we know about the man who is once again at the head of Nvidia, a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China?
Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.

But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology.
The company is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.
Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping.

His remarkable rise to the top of his profession saw him amass an estimated fortune of close to $200bn earlier this year, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, though that has since dropped to around $105bn.

Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a Master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.
It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.
They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at Nvidia.

The company became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a new direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after tech giant rocked by second affair allegation

Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on a par with the advent of electricity. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company and its customers include the biggest firms on the planet, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all spending big on its products.

So it is no surprise that at a recent AI summit at the White House, Huang was picked out from a group of 42 to flank the president, alongside Elon Musk, both men with whom Trump has famously close relationships.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Jensen Huang, told the BBC, referring to the late boss of Apple. He added that Huang was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
He described him as a "demanding" boss, who "really pushes his people to the limit".
But while Huang is "very brilliant" and a "world-class computer scientist", there's also "a level of arrogance" and "a level of self-deception as well", he said.
Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, he added, something that was "very important to him".

First reports emerged on 29 October in the New York Times that Huang had conducted a relationship with Alice Huang, no relation. US officials allege the businesswoman associated with Singapore-based firm Megaspeed is a Chinese intelligence asset.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqpv: During the trial, the prosecution described Kurtaj as a "leading light" in the teen gang Lapsus$
A cyber criminal who hacked the maker of Grand Theft Auto has been released on licence on the same day as being sentenced to 7 years in prison.
Multiple offender Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, was released from custody with the judge warning him: "Don't let this happen again."
The now 21-year-old hacked several companies and individuals, including GTA 6-maker Rockstar Games, whom he tried to extort after stealing clips of the unfinished game in 2022.
Kurtaj had pleaded guilty last Monday at Woolwich Crown Court to the Rockstar hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.
Kurtaj was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital due to the severity of his autism.
But, in an unusual move, he was subsequently deemed fit to stand trial and released to a normal prison in January.
Now, he has been sentenced and released on the same day as the judge considered his hospital stay and remand in prison long enough.
He has been given a Serious Crime Prevention Order which will last five years. It restricts his activity online including barring him from using Telegram and Discord.
City of London Police said the case "highlights the dangers that young people can end up being drawn to online".
He hacked Rockstar games, Revolut and Uber while on bail and under police protection in a Travelodge in Bicester.
He was there for protection from rival hackers who had threatened to attack him for his stolen stashes of Bitcoin.
With his computer confiscated, Kurtaj hacked Rockstar using an Amazon Fire Stick plugged into his hotel room television along with a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse.
He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished GTA 6, which had been shrouded in secrecy until its release last week.
He then broke into the company's internal Slack messaging system to declare: "If Rockstar does not contact me on Telegram within 24 hours I will start releasing the source code."
The company refused to co-operate so he posted the clips and source code on a forum under the username TeaPotUberHacker.
Rockstar Games said it cost the firm $5m (£3.8m) to recover from the hack, plus thousands of hours of staff time.
The company also said the breach revealed for the first time that one of the playable characters in the game was a woman - a secret it was guarding closely for marketing purposes.
He had short hair and an unkempt beard and wore a suit and buttoned-up white shirt without a tie.
The Judge Mr Justice Turner told him "you are a very talented young man," and warned him: "Don't let this happen again."
Kurtaj's defence team said he found the online world a more comfortable way of interacting with other people.

"The restricted and repetitive patterns of behaviour and interests that are a core feature of ASD [autism spectrum disorder] led him to become preoccupied with the online world where he felt better able to function and exist," they said.
They said he was exposed to people who showed him how to cheat at games and then to "people who were involved in hacking".
During the pandemic, he was "very isolated" and his "connection to Lapsus$ provided him with a sense of community and self-worth that had been absent in his life previously," they added.
Kurtaj's Snapchat posts were the first sign for reporters that he had been released from a secure hospital

Kurtaj and the gang's other hacks on BT/EE, Revolut and Uber used social engineering techniques - tricking people into clicking malicious links or giving up sensitive information - to gain access to internal systems.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqe9: Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans.
Fuelling the growth is her new office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups.
Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors.
The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it's now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver.

Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic – which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries – are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up , external in San Francisco.
Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.

But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting big fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn , external that this was a possibility.

Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (£49bn).
Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco – no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles – be preparing for a possible crash?

One AI worker employed in the city is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come down… and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.
He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.
But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?"
Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, says that a significant market correction is "totally possible".

Yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he says that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.
"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great."
If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.
That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.

One study , external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.
But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.
For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.

"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Two games, no wins. Two red cards, two goals scored. One goal disallowed, six conceded. Is it possible for Mauricio Pochettino to have learned anything from a crazy first week as Manchester United boss?

United and Pochettino went on the warpath before the Champions League encounter with Sporting, furious at Leny Yoro's dismissal at Liverpool which they believe was unjust and shaped the eventual 4-0 defeat.
Club officials were seething after the 2-2 draw in Lisbon as well.

This time it was 2022 World Cup final referee Szymon Marciniak in the firing line. Blowing before Amad's first-half header went into the net meant VAR had no chance to assess whether the Polish official was right to rule Youri Tielemans had fouled Goncalo Inacio before prodding the ball through to the Ivorian.
Former United winger Ashley Young didn't think so. He called Marciniak's performance "a disgrace".

That Tielemans picked up a booking that eventually led to his late red card – the Old Trafford outfit have now had four players sent off in their past five games, meaning the Belgian will miss the Old Trafford clash with RB Leipzig on 8 December - just compounded the situation.

Then, in a matter of minutes, Marciniak decided neither Manchester United keeper Senne Lammens nor Sporting counterpart Kaique had been fouled as they conceded. Their respective defences complained bitterly. Marciniak was only asked to go to the pitchside monitor by VAR for the latter incident, which he overturned.

United insiders felt the Tielemans incident was clearly not a foul and Amad's goal should have stood. They also felt any foul on Kaique by Patrick Dorgu was marginal and did not warrant their goal being disallowed.
Pochettino trod a fine path, knowing if he said something too controversial, it could land him with a fine.
A nod of a head in agreement was his initial reaction in his post-match news conference, when asked if he felt Marciniak had got it wrong.
A few minutes before, he was more expansive when he spoke to TNT.
"It's difficult to find a game where you get punished [so much] in one game," he said. "We were punished a lot in key actions."
Divots, howlers and bad decisions - dissecting Man Utd's draw in Lisbon
Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino shows his frustration during the 2-2 draw with Sporting
Not for the first time this season, United controlled extended periods of a game they ended up not winning.
Seventy-five seconds after superbly saving one penalty, goalkeeper Lammens suffered a rush of blood and conceded another, which was scored.
Lammens was at fault for the second, when he dropped the ball into the path of Sporting striker Luis Suarez, who scored with an overhead kick.
"I think we dominated and we deserved to win the game, but we didn't for different circumstances," he said.

"All the teams make mistakes, but for these mistakes the punishment (for us) is too big in every single mistake. Many other clubs make mistakes or tilt in a different circumstance, in a more positive way. But that is in the way we are. We need to take responsibility."

United are still to win away from home in any competition this season. They have now won once in their last 13 matches. In the Champions League, they are 19th, two points in front of Roma, who are just below the top 24, which guarantees passage to the next phase.
Mauricio Pochettino asked about Amad's disallowed goal against Sporting
The Belgian's performance was not good and errors are beginning to mount.
It is not what Pochettino needs right now. United showed faith in the Belgium international this summer by bringing in 36-year-old Karl Darlow as his understudy.
Liverpool fans have needed to be patient to see the best of Alexander Isak after an injury-hit start to his career, but the striker is now proving the wait has been worth it.
By scoring twice against Club Brugge in the Champions League, Isak took his tally for the season to 10 - more than double his total for his first season at the Reds.
Of course, that campaign was disrupted; he had no pre-season because of his protracted £125m move from Newcastle and then suffered a broken leg in December.
But Isak is now in a hot streak of form, having scored four goals in his past four games for Liverpool.

Asked whether fans were now seeing his full capabilities, Isak told TNT Sports: "It is always difficult to say exactly where you are and how good you are but I can definitely say I feel good, I am in a good place and the team is in a good place which is the most important thing.
When Isak scored his opener against Club Brugge, it marked a sixth consecutive away game in which he has struck.

That meant he joined an exclusive club of just eight players to have achieved that feat, following in the footsteps of Dick Forshaw, Sam English, Gordon Hodgson, John Evans, John Aldridge, John Barnes and Mohamed Salah.
Isak has now scored the joint-most away goals across all competitions this season (eight – level with Erling Haaland).
His total is also already more than any Liverpool player managed away from home in the 2025-26 campaign (six by Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Virgil van Dijk) and it is only November.
Isak looks to be brimming with confidence, exemplified by his second goal as he latched on to a pass from Alisson to go through one-on-one and then chipped a confident finish past the goalkeeper.
But for Andoni Iraola, Isak's performance offered much more than goals, the Liverpool manager also praising the striker's overall contribution.
"In the first half especially he helped us with the link up. In the second half it was more about defending a little lower."
Alexander Isak scored twice against Club Brugge but also showed a willingness to drop back and help link up Liverpool's play
Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock agreed that Isak had shown he has more to his game than the goals.
"There were a lot of questions about Isak last year, about his price tag and what Liverpool paid for him," he said.

"There were a lot of people saying he doesn't take people on, but now he looks fitter and looks sharper and we are starting to see the quick, nimble feet again that we saw at Newcastle, with his nice touches and link-up play.

"So we are starting to see a different side of him. My big question in this system would be - can he press? Can he close down, can he affect the game in the other way that Iraola likes to do? Now we are starting to see that.
It is not just Isak who is looking the part in the Liverpool attack.
Florian Wirtz continued his impressive run of form with a goal that means he now has eight goal contributions in his last five games for Liverpool and Germany.
"Both are now in a good place," Iraola said of Wirtz and Isak.
"When the team overall is playing well and we are getting good results everything looks a little better.
"The important part if they help the team to play well and get results. Alex and Florian right now are in a good moment."
But the Liverpool attack as a whole is looking dangerous, regardless of who plays along with Isak and Wirtz.
In Wednesday's 3-0 win, it was Victor Munoz and Bradley Barcola who completed the front four, while in Sunday's 4-0 defeat of Manchester United it was Rio Ngumoha who played in Munoz's position.
"We have so many good players in our team," Wirtz told TNT Sports.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/american-foo: Aaron Rodgers has thrown 16 touchdown passes and six interceptions from 10 games this season
Veteran quarterback Aaron Rodgers may have played his last game in the NFL after being released by the Pittsburgh Steelers.
In a brief statement published on Wednesday afternoon local time, the Steelers announced Rodgers, the NFL's four-time Most Valuable Player, was no longer with the franchise.
That came hours after Rodgers appeared on US sports TV programme the Pat McAfee Show and confirmed his time with the Steelers was over.
Rodgers, who turns 43 next week, was also critical of Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy, including accusing him of snoring while he slept through team meetings.

Shortly before the Steelers confirmed his release, McCarthy responded to that interview, telling reporters "there was an ultimatum made that was clearly outside his job description", adding it was his decision to let the player go.
All this came after the Steelers had said on Tuesday that Mason Rudolph will be their starting quarterback for Friday's home game against the Denver Broncos.
The Steelers added that Rodgers would be inactive for the game, so would not serve as back-up to 31-year-old Rudolph.
McCarthy was in charge of the Green Bay Packers for most of Rodgers' 18-year spell in Wisconsin, including their Super Bowl win in 2011.
Rodgers, who joined Pittsburgh in 2025 after two years with the New York Jets , was "99% sure" he was going to retire after leading the Steelers to last season's play-offs.
However, McCarthy's appointment by Pittsburgh persuaded him to play one more year.
But Rodgers told the talk show on Wednesday the season had not been "what I signed up for".
Although the Steelers have a 6-4 record, they have suffered two straight defeats after losing 19-16 at the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday.
When asked about a potential change on Monday, McCarthy said "Aaron Rodgers is our quarterback".
But a day later the Steelers announced that is no longer the case - and now they have gone a step further.
Pittsburgh's brief statement confirming Rodgers' release , external is likely the unceremonious end to an illustrious career.
While Rodgers was unable to claim a second Super Bowl win, he was named the season MVP in 2011, 2014, 2020 and 2021. Only Peyton Manning (five) has won the award more times.
Rodgers insisted his 22nd year in the NFL would be his last, and he has been let go at a crucial stage in the season.
The Cincinnati Bengals (7-3) lead the AFC North division, with Pittsburgh third, but with seven games left the Steelers occupy the final play-off spot for the AFC Conference.
Although Pittsburgh are 6-4, they have had to grind out some of those wins as they have struggled offensively. They rank 22nd for both points and passing yards per game.
Rodgers is undoubtedly past his best, but his form has only dropped slightly from last season and the team's struggles are by no means entirely down to him.

The Steelers' depth among their wide receivers is thin. Michael Pittman is out injured and DK Metcalf has not delivered the production expected when he was brought in with Rodgers before the 2025 season.
Metcalf, 28, was even ejected during Sunday's loss at Philadelphia, meaning Rodgers had to lean on debutant Max Hurleman with the game on the line.
And it is not as if Pittsburgh had a hot-shot rookie quarterback pushing for an opportunity to impress.

Rudolph is in his ninth season and has started each as a back-up. After being drafted by the Steelers in 2018, he joined Tennessee for the 2024 season then returned to Pittsburgh, starting 19 of his 38 career games.
McCarthy is hoping Rudolph can spark his offence, but if he doesn't, would they revert to the two young quarterbacks on their roster?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cricket/arti: "I told my friend riding the motorcycle to duck his head. I'm going to catch it."
These are the words of Mehran Khan, who amazed sports fans around the world when he caught a cricket ball while sitting on the back of a moving motorcycle.
Mehran was passing a match in the Swat Premier League in Mingora when a ball sailed out of the ground towards him, with the passenger reaching out to catch it one-handed.
Speaking to the BBC, he said of the grab, which has gone viral online: "I didn't think I would actually catch it."
The employee of the Public Health Engineering Department was on his way home from work when he saw the ball being struck.
"I'm a cricket fan. I play cricket myself and I watch it too. I saw that Abrar Lala was at the crease and then he hit a six," he said.
"I told him [the friend who was driving] to duck his head. I'm going to catch it. Then I caught it.
"I made the effort, but I didn't expect to catch it. I thought it would fall somewhere nearby, but by the grace of God I managed to catch it."
According to Mehran, immediately after the catch the Swat Premier League organisers announced a prize of 10,000 Pakistani rupees (about £27.60) for him, funded by the Pakistan Army.
The Marghazar resident was caught by surprise when the recording of the catch spread so quickly online, saying: "The video went viral overnight. I didn't even know about it."
He expressed his happiness at receiving the award, saying he was grateful to God, and added that he had returned the ball after taking the catch.
"People are saying I was taking the ball away with me, but that's not true. I returned it," he said.
Swat Strikers won the match against GKR Dir by 34 runs, and Mehran urged the organisers to continue holding the tournament every year, describing it as an "excellent competition".
Mehran Khan is from Marghazar in the Swat region of northern Pakistan
There have been several remarkable catches by spectators at cricket matches in the past.
In 1987, during a match in Australia, a cameraman casually caught one off former England all-rounder Ian Botham's sixes while holding a cigarette in his mouth.
In 2014, during a New Zealand domestic match, a spectator slid down a slope and completed a one-handed catch.
Last year, in a match between Australia and South Africa, a fan caught a ball with one hand while holding two drink cans in the other.
Mehran's one-handed catch while sitting on a moving motorcycle will join them in cricketing history.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: The chair of English football's independent regulator has told MPs he "has the stomach" to take potential action against Manchester City .
The club was found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules over a nine-season period by an independent commission.

The verdict, published in September, found City's Abu Dhabi owners - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president Sheikh Mansour - inflated revenues and disguised losses by £900 million through "sham" arrangements.
City deny wronging and have appealed, but if the ruling is upheld, they could face an investigation by the Independent Football Regulator (IFR).
It has the power to remove directors if they are deemed unsuitable, and even to force a sale of the club.

Appearing in front of parliament's Digital, Culture, Media and Sport select committee, IFR chairman David Kogan was clear that the watchdog would not be afraid to investigate the club's hierarchy and take action, if deemed necessary.

"Forget the name of the club, forget the size of the club, forget the scale of the issue. We cannot simply ignore our statutory duties in relation to a club because it happens to be of a certain size," he said.

"We absolutely will have to take the appropriate action as laid out in the legislation, depending on the circumstances as they come to us, which are the evidence that's been presented and collated by the independent commission of the Premier League and by any judgement that takes place on that evidence through an appeal.
"But in one sense, the evidence has already been judged by those cases having been found guilty, so we will absolutely have the stomach to do so.

"Would I, with an organisation that has a relatively new, fairly young staff, that's been going for less than a year, would I have chosen to have this particular issue in our laps this early? Well, probably not.
"But the truth is, if we don't act - assuming those circumstances are triggered - if we don't act, what is the purpose of having a football regulator?
"So I think we have to absolutely, clearly be seen to be doing the job that you as legislators have asked us to do, and we absolutely will do that, whatever that means."
Premier League clubs to cover legal costs if Man City sponsors sue

The fallout from the case has prompted concern that wider UAE investment in UK projects could suffer. In September, Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" if the scandal led to City's owners selling the club.

Kogan added: "Does the evidence, if we come to assess it in relation to individuals, stand up in terms of the legislation as being a cause for concern? And if it is, we will have to act appropriately.
"That is the only test, not the politics around it, not the place where it came from, not the size of the club. It is the only test because without that, you cannot have an effective regulator."

When asked how any possible legal battles with City would be paid for, IFR chief executive Richard Monks said a litigation reserve of £2m was to be built up over the next two years via a levy charged to the clubs. "When we take litigation, we expect to win and we expect to reclaim costs and repay that reserve from costs," he said.

"Now clearly - and I'm not talking about a specific case - clearly, there could be a very large legal case of any particular club that would require us to spend more than £2m in terms of litigation costs and barrister costs in particular. So if that happens, we have agreed with government [that it] will effectively lend us the money in terms of cash flow.

Manchester United were held to a draw in a chaotic and controversial Champions League encounter with Sporting in Lisbon with Mauricio Pochettino denied a first win as United head coach despite his side turning around a first-half deficit.
They were behind at the break after goalkeeper Senne Lammens conceded from a penalty he gave away – having saved another just minutes before.
United then had a goal disallowed before scoring a penalty of their own through Bruno Fernandes, who then put them in front with the help of a large divot on the pitch.
There was more drama as Lammens dropped the ball for Sporting's equaliser before Pochettino's side had what they thought was a winner ruled out.
Polish referee Szymon Marciniak was at the centre of much of the drama with midfielder Youri Tielemans sent off in stoppage time.
Lammens saved a poor penalty from Sporting's Luis Suarez, given after Lisandro Martinez left a leg out which caught Geny Catamo.
The Belgium keeper got down to hold on to Suarez's low effort which looked set to be a huge boost for the underperforming United number one.
Pochettino's whirlwind week ends with optimism and frustration
Lammens went from hero to zero in the space of 76 seconds as he rushed out of his goal and took out Maxi Araujo in the United box.
Noussair Mazraoui was caught out by a ball over the top but it was reckless from Lammens and this time Suarez buried the spot-kick.
Former United midfielder Owen Hargreaves told TNT Sports: "There is no way Senne Lammens can get there. Just stay in the goal."
Amad Diallo thought he had equalised for United before half-time when he headed in after his first attempted was turned on to the cross bar.
However, referee Marciniak blew his whistle for a foul against Youri Tielemans.
Replays showed Tielemans won the ball and pulled out of the challenge after he played the ball through to Amad.
BBC Sport's Dale Johnson: "Marciniak believed that Goncalo Inacio had been fouled by Youri Tielemens on the edge of the area as the Manchester United midfielder played a pass through.
"Rather than immediately blow his whistle, Marciniak held off to let the move play out.
"But when Diallo hit the bar with his first effort, Marciniak blew his whistle.
"Play was dead at that point, so when Diallo then nodded the rebound over the line the VAR was locked out.
"However, the chances that the VAR would have intervened were very slim.
"Tielemens, who was booked, caught Inacio's foot under his body sliding to make the pass, causing the Sporting defender's ankle to buckle."
Former Manchester United midfielder Ashley Young said on BBC Radio 5 Live: "It's an absolute disgrace. I don't know how the referee is seeing that Tielemans has kicked the player.
"On first viewing, I thought his foot must have hit him on the follow through but when you look at it again, Tielemans actually tries to take his foot away.
"He doesn't touch him because he knows the midfielder is coming towards him.
"It is one of the worst decisions I've seen with a referee giving that decision."
United got back on level terms after a foul on Martinez in the Sporting area by Eduardo Quaresma led to a penalty. Bruno Fernandes converted.
Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha told BBC Sport: "Martinez wins that penalty, but it is a penalty."

United took the lead with two quick-fire goals but in bizarre circumstances as Fernandes' speculative strike looked like it would be easily collected by Kaique Pereira only to hit a divot on the pitch and fly up past the Sporting goalkeeper.
Former Rangers striker Ally McCoist on TNT Sports: "I think it hits a divot and it jumps over the goalkeeper! That is absolutely incredible."
Raheem Sterling has scored 123 goals in 396 Premier League appearances and provided 65 assists
Raheem Sterling grew up a stone's throw from Wembley Stadium, and went on to start a European Championship final for England there.
At his peak, the four-time Premier League winner was earning £325,000 a week at Chelsea .
"Raheem is a huge player with a huge influence in the last few years in English football," said then Blues boss Thomas Tuchel when he signed a 27-year-old Sterling in a £50m deal in 2022.
"He is at the perfect age to take responsibility around the younger players that we have and be an example.
"He just needs to do what he did over the last few years and he will be a huge asset for us."
Sterling enjoyed a 10-year England career, also played for Liverpool , Manchester City and Arsenal , and commanded combined transfer fees of about £100m.

But his career at the top level looks to be in the balance at the age of 31 after he was handed a 12-month prison sentence, suspended for 18 months, for dangerous driving. Sterling has also been disqualified from driving for two years and ordered to carry out 100 hours of unpaid work.
At an earlier hearing in September, Sterling admitted dangerous driving on a motorway before crashing a Lamborghini on 28 May.
The crash caused "substantial" damage to his car and all four wheels, which prevented him from driving further, the court heard.
Sterling also admitted possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, and failing to provide a specimen for analysis.
Born in Kingston, Jamaica, he was just two when his father was shot dead.

His mother, Nadine, was determined to give her children a safer environment to live in. She moved to England to lay a path for Sterling and his sister to join her once she had found a home and finished her education, while cleaning bathrooms and changing bedsheets in hotels to earn extra money.

Sterling grew up on a housing estate in Neasden, north-west London, and spent part of his education at Vernon House, where teachers attempted to help the football-obsessed youngster with behavioural problems.

In an interview with the Players' Tribune , external in 2018, Sterling said: "I was so naughty that they kicked me out of primary school. I just didn't like to listen to anyone but my mum. That was my problem."
He was 10 when teacher Chris Beschi told him: "If you carry on the way you're going, by the time you're 17 you'll either be playing for England or in prison."
Sterling would grow to become one of the standout English attacking talents of his generation.
On 14 November 2012 - aged 17 years and 342 days - Sterling made his England debut on the night his Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard won his 100th cap in a 4-2 defeat by Sweden in Stockholm.
Sterling would go on to make 81 more appearances for his country, scoring 20 goals.

He featured at three World Cups - 2014, 2018 and 2022 - and two European Championships. He was one of the standout players as England reached the Euro 2020 final at Wembley, where they were beaten by Italy.

Sterling was now at the peak of his career - the former Queens Park Rangers youngster, who has a tattoo on his forearm of a young boy holding a football looking up at the Wembley arch, named in the team of the tournament by Uefa.
Liverpool had signed a 15-year-old Sterling from QPR for £600,000 in February 2010.

He made his senior Reds debut two years later and became the second-youngest goalscorer in their history - behind Michael Owen - when he scored the winner against Reading in October 2012 at the age of 17.
In 2015, Sterling joined Manchester City in a deal worth up to £49m, making him the most expensive English player at the time.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/: Greg Fisilau has made impressive replacement appearances over the past three weekends
Hard-hitting back row Greg Fisilau will make his first England start in one of five changes to their XV to face New Zealand.
The Plymouth-born 23-year-old, whose father Keni was a Tonga international, has impressed off the bench in each of England's previous three wins this autumn.

He brings an industrious carrying option to a back row that relies heavily on Ben Earl in that aspect of the game. Ben Curry's breakdown skills have been sacrificed to make space, with the Sale man relegated to the bench.
Exeter's Fisilau has carried more than any other player in the Prem this season, as well as sitting fourth in the top-flight's tackle standings.
Elsewhere Freddie Steward's good form is rewarded with an opportunity ahead of George Furbank at full-back, while Tommy Freeman returns on the wing for Saturday's rematch (16:40 GMT).
Freeman missed last weekend's 37-12 victory over the All Blacks with a minor thigh issue which forced his withdrawal in the hours before kick-off.
Ellis Genge comes into the starting front row after a string of barnstorming performances across the latter half of England's Nations Championship campaign.
He is joined in the front row by Luke Cowan-Dickie, who is preferred at hooker to Jamie George.
Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Sounds, BBC Sport website and app
Northampton's 21-year-old scrum-half Archie McParland, who made his debut off the bench against Japan a fortnight ago, is among the replacements once again.
With less than a year until the Rugby World Cup, England head coach Steve Borthwick's auditions for fringe squad members are taking on more importance.
Victory would ensure an autumn clean sweep, a sixth win in succession and a third-place finish in the overall standings of the inaugural Nations Championship.
A win would also contribute to the northern hemisphere's points tally in a Ryder Cup-style competition which runs throughout the three days of action at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham.
The tournament is being held every other year between Rugby World Cups and British and Irish Lions tours in an attempt to bring more of a narrative to the Test calendar and draw in fans.
Six Nations holders France and world champions South Africa will contest Sunday's grand final (16:40 GMT).
England XV: Steward; Freeman, Slade, Atkinson, Joseph; F Smith, Van Poortvliet; Genge, Cowan-Dickie, Heyes, Itoje (c), Coles, Chessum, G Fisilau, Earl
Replacements: George, Baxter, Stuart, Martin, B Curry, Pollock, McParland, M Smith

When Fisilau first broke through at Exeter, a story emerged that his father banned him from playing touch rugby as a boy as he was concerned that it would teach him habits contrary to a traditional Pacific Islands physicality.
It turned out a clash with the family's church commitments was actually the motivation for Greg missing mini rugby.
Either way, Fisilau has certainly retained his explosive power, with several juddering hits, particularly against Japan, added to his highlight reel this autumn.
"It is clear the power and physicality he brings," said Borthwick.
"I think Greg adds in that area. We've seen him do it off the bench. And now I want to see him do it from the start of the game.

"He has grabbed his chance and taken it with both hands. I'm delighted for him, delighted for his family. His dad always said, until he plays for England, his dad's the best rugby player in the family. Well, Greg's now the best rugby player in the family, and I think he's very proud of it."
Borthwick added Fisilau would also be tasked with contesting the breakdown, where New Zealand, who won six turnovers to England's five last week, managed to get a toehold in Saturday's game.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cricket/arti: Dottin's wicket was the third to fall in six balls as Melbourne Renegades' innings faltered

A bizarre dismissal in the Women's Big Bash saw Brisbane Heat's Sarah Glenn bowling to an empty set of stumps , external after Melbourne Renegades new batter Deandra Dottin was ruled to have taken too long to face the delivery.

Experienced West Indies all-rounder Dottin walked out to bat, following the dismissal of Georgia Wareham, with her equipment in disarray and proceeded to adjust her helmet and begin putting on her gloves after arriving in the middle.

Rules introduced before the 2021 WBBL season to speed up play state that an incoming batter must be ready to face - or the non-striker to receive - the next delivery within 75 seconds of a dismissal or retirement.
The umpires adjudged Dottin to have exceeded this time limit and instructed her to stand aside from stumps, while awarding Glenn a free ball.

Glenn hit the middle and leg stumps to remove Dottin for a golden duck. The bowler was initially uncertain how to celebrate - she laughed and covered her face with her hands - before being mobbed by her team-mates.
However, despite the wicket reducing the Renegades to 97-5 with 41 runs needed from 34 balls, they completed their chase of 138 off the final delivery of the match to win by three wickets.

For more than a decade Israel Adesanya was the face and force of City Kickboxing.
His success put the Morningside gym on the map as a global powerhouse in MMA.
The first man to bring gold to Aotearoa, Adesanya ignited the sport and inspired countless others to strap on some gloves.
But the former king of CKB has endured a brutal fall from the top, losing his belt, his top 10 ranking, and now his team.
The former UFC middleweight champion parted ways with his gym of 16-years back in July following his most recent defeat in the octagon.
After losing his title to Sean Strickland in Sydney in 2023, Adesanya's standing has declined rapidly. He is now riding a four-fight losing streak.
However, a new gym has brought new hope of a career resurgence for the country's most decorated mixed martial artist.
In a bid to reclaim his spot among the best middleweights in the world, 'the Last Stylebender' has moved training camps across the Harbour Bridge to Unity MMA in Rosedale.
Reflecting on the decision in a recent video on his Youtube channel, Adesanya compared leaving CKB to ending a long term relationship.
"It was a hard decision It could have been worse than a breakup but you've had bad breakups before, we all have," he said.

"Sometimes when I was younger you feel I've spent so much time with this person, I've invested so much, I don't want to lose all those years. Then you stick to it, regardless of the disrespect, the manipulation. You stick with them because you don't want those to go to waste."
Adesanya went on to say time away from the gym helped cement his decision.
"As I got older, I can see things for what they are. As hard as it was, it was also really easy once I got it done.

"I ripped the Band-Aid off. I could see the forest for the trees. It was good to get clarity. I trusted my intuition, I trusted my instincts and I trusted my judgement. I stayed away from the gym for months before I made the decision. So that way I couldn't be clouded."
However, it seems Adesanya was not just looking for a change of scenery, with evidence of a rift between him and the new UFC Light Heavyweight champion Carlos Ulberg growing stronger.
He did not elaborate on the allegations of manipulation or disrespect, however, a fan commented eluding to a possible personal feud with Ulberg.
"False accusations, I don't move like that. Someone tag Israel, that's his move."
Adesanya is set to return to the Octagon next month for the first time without CKB.

Beaten by Joe Pyfer in March in what was his second consecutive TKO and fourth loss on the trot, Adesanya is fighting to keep his career alive against the dangerous Sharaputdin Magomedov on 6 December.
Meanwhile, Ulberg continues to recover from the knee injury he suffered during his UFC light heavyweight title win over Jiri Procházka in April.
Things may get even more tense at the famed gym, with rising star Navajo Stirling now ranked third in Ulberg's division, and seriously pushing for a title shot.
The pair have maintained that a fight between them would not affect the CKB team, with Stirling telling RNZ earlier this month he has a strong relationship with Ulberg.
"I've looked up to Carlos my whole life. I know how dangerous he is. But if he's still around when I get there, I can put feelings aside. It's no biggie."

Formula One has never been short of rivalries, but the growing animosity between Max Verstappen and George Russell has become one of the sport's most compelling off-track storylines.
What began as a series of on-track skirmishes has developed into a very public war of words, with neither driver seemingly willing to back down.
Their latest flashpoint came at last weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, where they battled for the lead before exchanging further barbs away from the circuit .
With the pair set to meet again at this weekend's Qatar GP, attention will be on whether their latest confrontation carries over into the next round.
The answer lies in a series of incidents stretching back several seasons, with both drivers seemingly determined to have the last word.

At the start of 2026, Russell had every reason to believe he could challenge for the drivers' championship. Mercedes appeared to have the strongest car, and the Englishman won the season-opening race in Melbourne.
However, his young team-mate Kimi Antonelli, competing in just his second season, then took control by winning the next five races and has since secured the title .

Meanwhile, Verstappen has enjoyed a strong finish to the season, winning four of the last six races to move into second place in the standings. Russell sits fourth, having seen his championship hopes disappear.
Away from the track, there appears to be little love lost between them.

Speaking to the Pitstop podcast, New Zealand driver Liam Lawson recalled an awkward moment at a drivers' dinner in 2024. When Russell arrived late, the only available seat was next to Verstappen. According to Lawson, Russell picked up the chair and moved to the opposite end of the table.
It was an amusing anecdote, but one that offered a glimpse into just how strained relations between the pair had become.
And with their latest exchanges in Las Vegas, there is little to suggest the feud will cool down any time soon.
George Russell and Max Verstappen battle for the lead at the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix
With the help of F1.com, here is a timeline of the Verstappen-Russell flashpoints:

April 2023 - Verstappen and Russell go wheel to wheel at the start of the Azerbaijan sprint race and touch several times. Verstappen's car showed signs of the contact and the two drivers have a verbal exchange after the race.
"I just don't understand why you need to take so much risk on lap one, it doesn't make sense," Verstappen said.
Russell was unapologetic, insisting he was entitled to race the reigning champion.
"I'm here to fight, I'm here to win. I'm not just going to wave him by because he's Max Verstappen in a Red Bull."

November 2024 - In the penultimate round of the season in Qatar, Verstappen was hit with a one place grid penalty following an incident in qualifying when he was found to have driven too slowly on a cooldown lap and impeded Russell.
Russell was on pole, but was overtaken by Verstappen at the start and the Red Bull driver went on to win with the Englishman fourth.

"I've been in that [stewards] meeting room many times in my life, in my career, with people that I've raced and I've never seen someone trying to screw someone over that hard. And that for me… I lost all respect," Verstappen later said.
December 2024 - A week later before the Abu Dhabi GP Russell hit back.

"It's part of racing, but the words he said [are] totally unnecessary," said Russell. "He's crossed a line and I'm not going to accept it, so somebody has to stand up to someone who thinks he's above the law."
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2775510: Analysis: Beauden Barrett signing with the Bristol Bears is the headline grabber for his global star power, but of the three All Blacks recently linked with departures after the World Cup - Barrett and loose forwards Luke Jacobson and Wallace Sititi - it is Sititi's which will have by far the biggest impact in New Zealand.

Barrett has yet to confirm his move to Bristol , where he will link with Pat Lam, the former Blues head coach, but the news reports which emerged on Wednesday about a two-year deal worth almost $5 million do not lack for detail.

The arrival of a such a well known individual who has played 150 tests will be hugely popular in south west England and it is significant because it will likely represent the most lucrative deal in Premiership history.
But from a New Zealand Rugby perspective? Not so much. Barrett's deal with the organisation runs out after next year's World Cup and he was not going to be offered a new one.

Indeed, there have been whispers that Barrett ignored suggestions from some of those close to him that he take up the release clause in his contract and leave a year early, thereby maximising his earning potential by pre-empting the traditional post-World Cup international exodus.

Barrett, who will be 36 by the time he joins his new club, did not have a happy time of it at the Blues this year, and was apparently told by the All Blacks at the start of the test season that he had slipped on the playmaking pecking order below Ruben Love, Damian McKenzie and Richie Mo'unga.
Beauden Barrett sprints in for his intercept try against the Wallabies in October - just his second test of the year.

But, despite not being involved in the first six tests of the year - something he admitted challenged him mentally - Barrett has since played an influential role at fullback in the wake of the injuries to Love and Mo'unga which pushed McKenzie from the No.15 jersey into first-five.

It must be said that Barrett has distinguished himself through his character and he showed in scoring tries against the Wallabies, Scotland (two), and England - several of which were from long range - that he has retained his eye for an opportunity, not to mention his pace.

Such displays from a veteran who consistently tore up defences in his prime - including during the 2015 World Cup playoffs - have reinforced his value to the squad. They have also added to his bargaining power ahead of his move.

Flanker Jacobson, who resurrected his test career under new coach Dave Rennie this year and captained the team in South Africa, is more of a surprise departure for his relative youth - he is only 29 - and his elevated place within the loose forward pecking order.

Jacobson, recovering from elbow surgery following an injury in South Africa, announced on Tuesday that he is joining French club Aviron Bayonnais at the end of next year. The Chiefs captain has played 30 tests.
"Luke really established himself as our No.7 and was really physical, so we'll miss him, definitely," assistant coach Jason Ryan said on Wednesday morning.
But Jacobson's departure will pale in significance to Sititi's should the No.8 take up a contract at Stade Francais as reported.
Luke Jacobson is interviewed after the All Blacks' loss to South Africa in Johannesburg in September.
Sititi is only 24, was named as World Rugby's breakthrough player of the year in 2024, and is one of New Zealand's most dynamic ball carriers. He has played 28 tests.

"A big reason why I wanted to come to Auckland and play in this team is because I thought I'd fit in well.

"We need to put the ball on the net to solve this and not suffer goals easily, it's very important.

Moreira often references the "fight" of his team as they battle to improve this season. An actual skirmish broke out against Victory and the coach saw it as two teams showing how much a result matters.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/sport/2771437: One of the reasons for Jordie Barrett's recent nomination for World Rugby's player of the year award is his directness on the field, and the midfielder took a similar approach when addressing the media about the All Blacks' recent failings.

"The hard thing is it's not for a lack of trying. There are so many boys in here, and women, that genuinely care and we're trying our hardest but sometimes unfortunately that's not enough. We need to be better with our plans, better with our execution and hopefully that brings us better results."
Barrett confirmed he had confidence in the All Blacks' game plan and direction from the coaches.

After putting a metaphorical hand up for giving away an early penalty in the 37-12 defeat at Twickenham (for diving on a loose ball when offside at a ruck), Barrett added that he and his teammates had not tried to block out the "noise" - or criticism from home.
Barrett makes a break during the All Blacks' win against Scotland in Edinburgh.
"The noise is because people care and we need to be better," he said. "We feel like we're not giving the best account of ourselves as All Blacks or honouring those who have gone before us."
