https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6m2: Baroness Cass said the current wording of the bill risked "serious unintended consequences"
The author of the independent review into gender identity services for young people says she does not support the current draft bill banning conversion practices - having previously welcomed it.
Baroness Cass told BBC Radio 4's Today programme while it is "desirable" to ban the practices, "the challenge is that we have not yet as far as I can see got a workable bill".

At a parliamentary committee scrutinising the bill, she also said it risked "serious unintended consequences" for parents of children suffering gender distress, or medical professionals working in that area.
They added they would take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as they "want to get this ban right". The government has said the bill would protect LGBT people in England and Wales.
Conversion practices are generally described as interventions, treatments or activities designed to change or suppress someone's sexual orientation or gender identity.
This can sometimes happen in religious or family settings and can be very distressing for the person at the centre of it.
There have been long-running campaigns in the UK to outlaw such practices, and in its 2024 manifesto, the Labour party promised to introduce a bill banning them.
When the government introduced its draft legislation , external in June this year, Baroness Cass was quoted in the publicity for it , external .

In it, she said: "I am pleased to see that the government is bringing forward legislation which not only gives a clearer definition of what conversion practices are, compared to previous drafts, but also what they are not."
She went on to say she looked forward to the bill receiving further scrutiny before it became law.
But asked at the Draft Conversion Practices Bill committee if she supported the bill's current form, she said simply "no".
Baroness Cass said the increased "polarisation" used in the debate around gender meant people may use the new law in a way that wasn't intended.

The current wording of the bill requires the victim to suffer "serious harm to the individual's physical or mental health, or serious alarm or distress to the individual which has a substantial adverse effect on their usual day-to-day activities".
But Baroness Cass said she worried this wording left open the possibility of "vexatious" complaints that could put therapists working with young gender-distressed people at risk of prosecution.
"Therapeutic interactions can be distressing and often are because you're discussing quite sensitive issues," she told the Today programme.
"So If a young person comes away feeling upset, distressed, angry, that might be the result of a quite appropriate therapeutic intervention but still could be judged as poor professional practice."
She told the committee that professionals working at the new NHS Gender Dysphoria Clinics were concerned that even complaints processes that didn't result in a prosecution could be damaging.
"The problem is the chilling effect of professionals knowing that they may be open to complaint, and indeed prosecution," she told the Today programme.
Baroness Cass also raised concerns about the possible impact the new law could have on families.

She said that, for instance, if a parent stopped a child's money if they thought they might buy a "breast binder or hormones" that this may also fall within the scope of the bill and result in prosecution.

Asked about her apparent support for the bill when it was first published, Baroness Cass said that she was in favour of the idea but had not had the time to read the details before the press release was to be published, but went ahead and gave the quote anyway.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqjd: Nicola Packer was acquitted of "unlawfully administering to herself a poison or other noxious thing" with the "intent to procure a miscarriage"
Women arrested or convicted for having illegal abortions will have their criminal records wiped as new automatic pardons come into force in England and Wales , external .

Ending the Victorian-era law should avoid traumatic experiences such as that of Nicola Packer, who was recently cleared by a jury after taking medication at home during a Covid lockdown. She had ended a pregnancy without realising she was around 26 weeks pregnant, far beyond the legal 10 week limit.
Her friend Helle Tumbridge told the BBC's Today Programme she had been "treated appallingly" until justice was served.

Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi, who brought forward the decriminalisation amendment last year, says the change will clear the names of more than 100 women who have been "unnecessarily harmed" by an "outdated" law.
Ms Packer, who was 41 at the time, took pills called mifepristone and misoprostol, which were prescribed over the phone due to Covid restrictions, to end a pregnancy in 2020.
Prosecutors alleged that she knew she had been pregnant for more than 10 weeks, which she denied.
Jurors deliberated for more than six hours to reach their unanimous verdict, clearing her name.
Speaking with the BBC and Nicola's consent, her friend Ms Tumbridge said the whole incident was "incredibly traumatic".
"Nicky had what's known as a cryptic pregnancy - that's when you don't have any sign of a pregnancy, no baby bump, no other symptoms.
"She thought she was just a few weeks pregnant and she sought an abortion and was prescribed that by the NHS. Unfortunately, she was a lot more far gone."
Nicola experienced a stillbirth and went to hospital. The staff there called the police.

"She was arrested. She spent a time in her hospital room recovering with two police officers present, one was a man. She was treated appallingly. She was made to use the toilet with the door open in front of the police officers."
It took five years of investigations for a trial to eventually find her not guilty.
"Of course, by that point the damage had been done," says Tumbridge, "and she'll live with that trauma for the rest of her life."
At the time, The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists said Nicola's trial demonstrated "just how outdated and harmful" that law was.
It is now no longer a criminal offence for a pregnant woman to terminate her own pregnancy at any stage.
Minister for Victims and Tackling Violence Against Women and Girls, Alex Davies-Jones, said pardoning women for abortion offences related to their own pregnancy had been a priority.
"I'm pleased to be able to commence the change that Parliament voted for.

"For those affected, I know that clear and accessible information about what happens next is vital. Women do not have to take any direct action themselves, but can find out more information online and contact our dedicated casework team."

Heidi Stewart, from the abortion care provider BPAS, said: "While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice."

Abortion in England and Wales is legal with an authorised provider up to 24 weeks, with very limited circumstances allowing one after this time, such as when the mother's life is at risk or the child would be born with a severe disability.
It is also legal to take prescribed medication at home if a woman is less than 10 weeks pregnant.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y: The capsule dissolves in the stomach and releases a small sponge which collects cells from the lining of the oesophagus as it's removed
Some people with bad and persistent indigestion should be offered quick "sponge in the gullet" tests to check for oesophageal cancer, new draft guidelines for the NHS in England recommend.
The sponge tests can be carried out in GP surgeries in minutes, and are less invasive than hospital endoscopy checks that instead use a small camera to look inside the body.
The tests are already available in some places but could now be offered across England.
Heartburn or acid reflux can occur with a condition called Barrett's oesophagus that increases the risk of cancer in the long term.

It is thought between one and two adults in every 100 has Barrett's oesophagus, where cells have started to change. Most won't go on to develop cancer, but demand for NHS endoscopy is high, meaning some with the condition aren't checked as often as recommended.
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) says the sponge tests, already offered in some places, could help give more patients peace of mind.

For the test, patients swallow a small dissolving capsule attached to a thread. Once in the stomach, it releases a tiny sponge. The sponge collect cells from the lining of the gullet as it is gently pulled back out of the patient's mouth by the doctor.

Prof Jonathan Benger, chief executive of NICE, says sponge tests offer a "quick and less invasive" way to detect concerning changes, helping to identify people who should go on to have further tests and treatment.

Prof Peter Johnson, national clinical director for cancer at NHS England, said: "The NHS is always looking for better ways to get to the bottom of people's symptoms, and thousands have already benefited from this incredibly efficient test through pilots we have been running, so it's fantastic it is now being considered for roll out across the country.

"Many people have acid reflux, and having an easier way to check for changes in the lining of the oesophagus can make a big difference for patients, reducing the need for more complicated endoscopy tests and helping the NHS free up resources to find cancers at an earlier stage."
However, no diagnostic test, including endoscopy, identifies every case and people who receive an all-clear sponge test result should still be monitored in the long term, NICE adds.
The sponge tests can help detect oesophageal cancer and Barrett's oesophagus in people with reflux disease.
The oesophagus leads to the stomach. Both are highlighed in red/orange
Reflux can cause heartburn, which is a burning sensation in the middle of your chest, as well as an unpleasant sour taste in your mouth, caused by stomach acid.
A lax or weakened sphincter at the bottom of the oesophagus or food pipe, where it meets the stomach, can be part of the issue, allowing digestive juices to seep up the wrong way.
Being overweight, smoking and drinking alcohol can increase a person's risk of reflux.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckvg: A GP has warned that long waits for ADHD and autism assessments are creating a situation where the people most in need are not being seen.
According to experts, demand has risen so sharply in recent years that it now far exceeds what the mental health system can cope with.
New figures seen by BBC Scotland News suggest more than 38,000 adults are waiting for neurodevelopmental assessments, with at least 14,000 of them waiting longer than two years.

Dr Marianne McCallum, who represents the Deep End group of doctors working in Scotland's most deprived areas, said it was a "tragedy" that people who really needed a diagnosis because they were not coping could not be seen by a specialist.
She said those who had the most to gain from a diagnosis were currently the least likely to get it, with a huge rise in private referrals creating a two-tier system.
Dr McCallum, who works in the Ferguslie Park area of Paisley, said: "It's just become a bit of a mess, because there's a bottleneck and the secondary services are overwhelmed.
"In primary care we're trying to hold a lot of this without any extra resource."
Dr McCallum said some patients were influenced by social media.
"I've had people who've come in saying they think they need an ADHD assessment and actually when I've spoken to them, the problem is dyslexia," she said.
She said this meant some people who had a really significant lifelong neurodevelopmental condition were unable to access services.
"It is a tragic situation, particularly for people who really could do with the diagnosis," Dr McCallum said.
"Sometimes they lose their job because they're not coping and they snap and that's it. So I think it is a tragedy."
Lynne Balmain is one of thousands of people in Scotland waiting for an NHS assessment for ADHD
Autism is a lifelong developmental condition that affects the way a person communicates, interacts, and processes information.
Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder , external (ADHD) can affect different brain functions including communication, emotions and attention.
Drugs that can help symptoms can only be prescribed by the NHS if the patient has an NHS diagnosis, or under what is called a "shared care" agreement.
Lynne Balmain is waiting for an NHS assessment after paying £1,000 for a private ADHD diagnosis from a clinic in Glasgow last year.
The 54-year-old said: "I wasn't sleeping at night, I was aware of the speed that my brain was functioning at, it was constant.
"I was catastrophising over simple day-to-day things that everybody does."
Lynne said she was currently paying for medication with no indication of when she will be seen by the NHS.
"I can't really afford to keep this going but from a mental health and well-being perspective, I can't afford not to be medicated either so I'm being forced to choose," she said.
In recent years, Scotland has seen an unprecedented rise in the number of people seeking assessment and support for both ADHD and autism.
But a 2025 report by the Royal College of Psychiatrists in Scotland (RCPsychiS) said there was no national approach to meeting that demand.

It also said those with more severe mental illness faced longer delays accessing urgent care.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c: The UK's seasons are changing, with fewer winter frosts and more hot summer days, according to new analysis from the Met Office.
Across the UK, the number of winter days with an air frost – when the air temperature falls to 0C or below – was around a quarter lower in the decade to 2025 than during the period from 1961 to 1990.
In southern England, the reduction was around a third while the average number of UK summer days reaching 25C has more than doubled.
The Met Office says climate change has led to these seasonal shifts.
"Our summer is getting wider and our winter is getting smaller," says Dr James Pope, climate scientist at the Met Office.
"The driver of this is that the whole global climate is warming. And that impacts on the UK.
"Some areas went from their wettest ever winter to a severe drought via a record-breaking summer for the whole country."
The changing conditions have affected wildlife and led some farmers to grow different crops.
Some of the biggest reductions in winter air frosts have been in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, where the average number of days has fallen by around 11 compared with 1961 to 1990.
Southern England has seen other significant changes. In Cornwall, the average number of winter air frost days has almost halved, falling from around 18 to just 10.
On the Isle of Wight, the figure has also fallen by almost half, from around 21 to 11 days.
Scotland remains the frostiest UK nation, but has also seen a reduction, from around 45 to 38 winter air frost days.
Summer days reaching 25C have become more common across the UK.
Some of the biggest increases have been in southern England, where the average number of summer days reaching 25C has more than doubled, from just over eight to more than 16.
In Essex and Suffolk, they have risen by almost 13 days in both counties.
The Met Office defines a hot day as one where the temperature reaches 30C or above.
Across the UK, the average number of these days has increased fourfold, from 0.3 to 1.2 per summer.
The increase is particularly striking in Greater London, where days reaching 30C have risen from an average of 1.3 to 6.1 per summer.
Summer 2026 was the hottest on record , according to provisional Met Office data.
There were five widespread heatwaves and 40 days of temperatures above 30C, smashing the previous record of 34 days.
Tim Young's onions have been smaller than usual making them harder to sell to supermarkets

"Humans, animals and crops are encountering extremes of temperature that we've not seen before and this is a physiological challenge to all three," says Thomas Crocker, science manager with the Met Office's climate security team.
This has led to water challenges, he says, with wet winters causing problems with planting, pests and diseases.
Dry summers have meant there has not been enough water to grow crops.
"The impact on horticulture is seismic, it's affected all crops," says John Walgate, CEO of British Growers, which represents most British horticultural organisations growing vegetable and fruit.
Walgate says this year's weather has been particularly tough for brassicas like cauliflowers, cabbages and broccoli, with yields down by about 50%.
Irrigated crops such as onions, potatoes and carrots also suffered from a lack of water due to low rainfall and hot temperatures.
It's not all been bad though. Walgate says soft fruit such as strawberries have had a "good year".
Tim Young and his family have been farming in Norfolk since the 1960s.
But his arable crops - onions, wheat and sugar beet - have been struggling because of the hotter, drier summers and fewer cold days in winter which kill bugs.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c: The sun shone on 2025's Thanksgiving Parade but the forecast this year is not so bright
Strong winds are threatening to disrupt Thursday's Thanksgiving parade in New York City for the first time since World War Two.

A potent Nor'easter storm could impact the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade which is due to be taking place for the 100th time, with the risk that it could be too windy for the event's iconic balloons to fly.

The US National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning, valid from 10:00 local time (15:00 GMT) on Thursday until 01:00 (06:00 GMT) on Friday with gusts potentially reaching 60mph (97km/h) - although the very strongest winds are likely to occur after the parade is due to end.
Heavy rain and coastal flooding will pose additional hazards across the eastern USA as the storm sweeps through, while some inland parts could also see snow.
Western areas of the country have also faced Thanksgiving travel headaches, with Pacific storms and coastal flooding.
Storms targeting both US coasts threaten to snarl Thanksgiving travel for millions
The parade started life as the Macy's Christmas Parade, organised by employees at Macy's department store in New York City in a bid to boost holiday sales.
The first event took place on Thanksgiving Day 1924. It has only been cancelled during World War Two, when it was put on hiatus between 1942 and 1944. As a result, this year marks the 100th parade.

It is due to take place from 08:30 local time (13:30 GMT), ending at around 12:00 (17:00 GMT) , and involves marching bands, street performers and floats parading through the streets of New York City, as well as 100 brightly-coloured inflatable balloons.
Confetti filled the air above this enormous turkey at the start of the 2025 parade
However, due to city regulations full-size balloons cannot fly if sustained winds exceed 23mph (37km/h), or in gusts of more than 35mph (56km/h).
There is a risk that Thursday will bring winds approaching those strengths.
However, record wind gusts also made the 1997 route a no-fly zone and the balloons were still featured in the parade.
The giant character balloons were tethered to golf carts that year.
In 1989, when a major snowstorm stopped balloon handlers getting to the parade route, the cheer and dance teams stepped in to pull the giant balloons along.
Over the last few days, a cluster of showers and thunderstorms has been swarming in the Gulf of Mexico.

That area of disturbed weather is now moving northwards, close to the east coast, and deepening into a potent area of low pressure - a Nor'easter storm, so called because it delivers strong north-easterly winds which drive into the east coast.
The National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning for New York City, as well as Long Island and north-east New Jersey.
It comes into force part-way through the parade and warns of strong to damaging wind gusts, which could affect trees and power lines and bring significant travel disruption.

The winds are forecast to strengthen through the day peaking during the evening, meaning the very strongest gusts are likely to hit after the parade is over. However, there is a risk that they could approach the threshold that would ground the balloons.
Up to 3in (75mm) of rain could fall with the risk of flooding, which could be exacerbated along the coast as high tides arrive on Thursday evening.
Large waves and high sea levels are expected, bringing the threat of erosion and damage along the shoreline.
Other eastern parts of the USA will also receive heavy rain and strong winds, with snow in some inland parts adding to the Thanksgiving travel headaches.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6x2: Historic space mission lifts off with first Pakistani astronaut aboard Chinese rocket

China launched its Shenzhou-24 space mission on Wednesday carrying three astronauts to its Tiangong space station, including Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to join a Chinese crewed space mission.
Beijing said it hopes the flight will strengthen ties with Islamabad, as the two countries mark 75 years of co-operation in space.
Speaking to reporters at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, Ali said he was "carrying the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis".
The mission, which also comprises of commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi, took off at 08:18 (00:18 GMT) from the Gobi desert. Minutes later, it was declared a "complete success".
While in space, the Shenzhou-24 crew will carry out experiments and test technology in fields like aerospace medicine, combustion and study the effects of space on living organisms.
The mission comprises of payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, flight engineer Wu Yi and commander Tang Hongbo
They will also study how the space environment affects aging, with the hope of developing new ways to prevent and treat age-related vascular diseases.
Ali will conduct studies on photosynthesis in bacteria and the effects of radiation and microgravity - a very weak gravity in space - on seeds.
The former fighter pilot will return to Earth after a short stay, with two other Chinese crew members who have been at the space station since May.

Tang and Wu will spend six months at Tiangong space station along with Zhu Yangzhu, a member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, which lifted off in May this year. Zhu has been studying how the human body adapts to long periods in space.
China has poured billions of dollars into its space programme and its prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.
It is now keen to show the world that the station has the potential to become an international research platform rather than an exclusive Chinese facility.
Hundreds of people gathered at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center before dawn waving Chinese and Pakistani flags.

This also comes at a time when Beijing is trying to establish itself as a major alternative to the US-led space programme, with a bold goal to land Chinese astronauts on the moon for the first time by 2030.
For Pakistan, which does not have its own spacecraft to send astronauts to space, being invited to be a part of this mission is significant.

Ali and Khurram Dawood, the other candidate to reach the final stage in the Shenzhou-24 crew selection, were trained in China and had worked in Chinese space stations under the supervision of Chinese experts.
Mastering the Chinese language was one of his "biggest challenges", Ali said, according to Pakistani media.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/c: Christmas Day is a month away and as the festive season approaches you may start to wonder - could 2026 be a 'white Christmas'?
Over the past 65 years, there have been 41 white Christmases, meaning we are more likely than not to see one somewhere in the UK.
Forecasting the chances of a month ahead of the big day is a bit like staring into a crystal ball - but are there any early omens of snow on the festive horizon?

For a Christmas to be officially declared as 'white', a single snowflake needs to be recorded falling at any point during 25 December, at any of the Met Office's network of around 300 weather stations.
It means there doesn't have to be a thick covering of snow on the ground to qualify.
Indeed, the landscape could be beautifully festive and white with lying snow, but if no new snow falls on Christmas Day it cannot technically be called a white Christmas.
The last widespread white Christmas was in 2010, when snow fell at 19% of measuring stations and a significant 83% of stations reported snow lying on the ground.
Every year from 2020 to 2023 was officially a white Christmas, however very few places actually reported settling snow.
In December 2010 the UK experienced low temperatures and significant snowfalls. Lying snow was reported in many places on Christmas Day
A number of factors will influence the UK's weather in the run-up to the festive season.
A major one is the record-breaking El Niño which is, scientists predict, approaching its peak in the Pacific.

El Niño's strongest impacts tend to be felt close to where the phenomenon occurs, in the tropical Pacific, but the energy it releases into the atmosphere can send ripples through weather patterns across the globe.

Strong El Niño events can increase the odds of wet and stormy weather during the late autumn and early winter, and some studies suggest they can raise the chances of colder weather later in the season - but the evidence from past El Niños is decidedly mixed.
Will El Niño and the polar vortex bring snow to the UK this winter?
Stormy autumn, cold winter - how might El Niño affect the UK weather?
Earlier in November the winds of the stratospheric polar vortex weakened and reversed, marking the earliest sudden stratospheric warming event on record.
This phenomenon tends to occur much later in winter and can - but doesn't always - weaken the jet stream, increasing the chance of cold northerly or easterly winds.
Occurring so early in the season, the effects this time are harder to quantify. It is not known what - if any - impact it will have on the weather over the weeks ahead.

The latest predictions from scientists at the Met Office , external , taking these and other factors into account, suggest there could be an increased likelihood of colder and drier-than-average conditions during the winter months of December, January and February.

However this only represents an increased probability of these conditions and - even if this occurs across the season as a whole - there are still very likely to be shorter-term periods of milder, wetter weather.
It is often tricky to accurately forecast snow in the UK, even a day or two in advance.
Snow requires just the right combination of cold air and moisture, and small changes in either of these elements can mean predicted snow actually falls as rain or vice versa.
It goes without saying that longer range snow forecasts are even more challenging and with Christmas still a month away it is impossible to offer precise predictions.
You can keep up to date with the latest forecast by checking BBC Weather online and the app .
Share your memories of white Christmas periods. What weather changes have you noticed over time?
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy0: As food inflation rises, vegetables are becoming an increasingly expensive part of the household budget
India's inflation is rising again. And the biggest worry is what's happening to food prices.
The latest government data , external shows retail inflation climbed to 6.09% in October, up from 5.54% in September.
But look more closely at food inflation. It has surged to 8.94%.
The squeeze was sharper in rural India, where food inflation was 9.09%, compared with 8.68% in urban areas.
In other words, food prices are rising considerably faster than the overall rate of inflation.
Food inflation this year has been driven by a combination of weather disruptions, supply shortages and rising input costs, say economists.

With nearly 60% of its farmland dependent on rainfall , external , India remains acutely vulnerable to the vagaries of the monsoon. This year, the southwest monsoon was 13% below normal and unevenly distributed, while intensifying El Niño conditions have heightened risks to farm production.
Onion prices have surged, adding to the pressure on household food budgets
A survey by polling agency LocalCircles found that six in 10 consumers say household essentials cost them over 20% more each month than a year ago, prompting calls for government intervention.
Rising prices are also forcing cutbacks: 74% are curbing discretionary spending on eating out, shopping and entertainment, while half are buying smaller quantities of essentials.
Food accounts for a smaller share of Indian household spending than it once did, but remains the biggest driver of inflation, with significant economic, social and political consequences.
In India's latest consumer price index, food and beverages account for 36.75% of the basket of goods and services used to measure inflation.
That is down sharply from 45.86% under the previous series, reflecting changing consumption patterns as Indians spend more on services, transport, healthcare, education and other non-food items.
Yet a sharp increase in food prices can move the overall inflation rate significantly, while disproportionately affecting people whose incomes leave little room for adjustment.

"Adjustability for a poor country like India is significantly lower," says Rajeswari Sengupta, an associate professor of economics at Mumbai-based Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, pointing to the fact that a substantial proportion of household income is still spent on food.
According to calculations by Dharmakirti Joshi, chief economist at analytics firm Crisil, the bottom 20% of rural households faced inflation of 6.9% in October, against 6.5% for the richest 20%.

Crisil's Roti Rice Rate analysis , external found that the cost of a home-cooked vegetarian thali - a meal platter - rose 12% year-on-year in October, driven by higher prices of onions, tomatoes, vegetables, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. A non-vegetarian thali became 9% more expensive.

Rice prices were up about 10% year-on-year, pulses 8%, edible oil 13% and LPG 10%, according to Pushan Sharma, director of intelligence at Crisil. "It's no longer a few commodities that are driving this increase, it's becoming a little more broad-based," he says.
When onion prices spike, households can cut back on their consumption to some extent. But substituting rice, pulses and cooking oil is considerably harder.

And food inflation is not just about what farmers produce. It is also about how efficiently that food is stored, processed and moved to the market. Weaknesses at each stage can turn seasonal shortages into sharp price spikes - and gluts into waste.
Onions, for instance, are particularly susceptible to seasonal price swings.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm93: Between 2013 and 2026, almost 250,000 badgers were killed in England as part of widespread culling to tackle bovine tuberculosis (TB)
Plaid Cymru ministers have ruled out a mass badger cull as part of updated plans to tackle bovine tuberculosis (TB).
It follows months of speculation over the Welsh government's intentions, after an expert group warned "a step change" was needed in efforts to eradicate the disease.
While farming leaders have long called for tougher badger controls, a petition against culling has attracted more than 28,000 signatures on the Senedd website in recent weeks.
The Welsh government said it would take "a new and pragmatic approach to TB eradication that is evidence-based and science-led".
While there will be no widespread cull, targeted measures are under consideration which could involve trapping and killing some badgers if they test positive for the disease.
But further research is needed first and no timetable has been set out.
Farming unions called for swifter action, while wildlife groups warned that killing badgers was "not off the table".
Latest figures show nearly 96% of cattle herds in Wales are now TB free.
But the problem - which can be devastating for affected farms - is concentrated, with higher incidence levels in west Wales and along the border with England.
There were 10,090 cows slaughtered following TB testing in the 12 months to June 2026.
Under the previous Labour-run Welsh government, a target was set for Wales to completely eradicate bovine TB by 2041.
But before May's Senedd election an expert group set up to advise ministers , external warned that goal would "not be met", and called for urgent action and more funding.
Cattle are slaughtered if they are found to be carriers of bovine TB
The Bovine TB Eradication Programme Board's latest recommendations were published on Tuesday, alongside the government's response.
On badgers, ministers said they were "not pursuing a mass, non-selective cull".
However further research is proposed of the role played by badgers and deer in spreading the disease via new population surveys and fieldwork.

This would then lead to developing "targeted and proportionate" interventions which could include trapping and testing badgers before vaccinating or euthanising them, "where the evidence supports this".

Localised trapping and culling was trialled in Wales on nine farms between 2017 and 2024, but the cost involved drew criticism after hundreds of thousands of pounds was spent on killing a small number of badgers.
Officials told a briefing for journalists that "selective removal" of badgers was a possibility in future, but "[we] cannot give you a timeline".
In July, the Senedd backed a Reform UK motion calling on the Welsh Government to consider targeted wildlife control, including badger culling
Changes to cattle testing were also being proposed by the government, to help spot infection earlier.
They will work with the farming industry to explore "safe ways" of moving cattle out of TB restricted herds, to help businesses continue to operate.
Farms experiencing persistent issues and under so-called enhanced management will be offered more choice in how their situation is handled.
There is talk of a new advisory service for farmers and vets - and moves to provide better, more up-to-date data on the latest disease risk.
For farming families "a TB breakdown can mean months or years of restrictions, uncertainty and difficult choices", said agriculture minister Llyr Gruffydd
Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability, Llyr Gruffydd MS, said bovine TB remained "one of the most serious animal health challenges facing Wales".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqzj: The waste was dumped over garden fences in South Wigston over several months
Two fly-tippers were able to dump huge amounts of household waste over their garden fences without being detected for several months, with the pile eventually reaching 20 tonnes.
It was spotted on land owned by a business in South Wigston, Leicestershire, earlier in the year.

However, due to the location of the fly-tip, it was not immediately visible to employees of the business, which Oadby and Wigston Borough Council said "allowed the offenders to act over several months".

The two individuals responsible were each issued with a £600 fixed penalty notice following an interview under caution, the authority added, while a third person was cautioned for their role in the offence.
Before the rubbish could be cleared, the council's environmental health officers worked with the business to gather evidence to prove who had been responsible.
The authority has not specified which business was affected by the fly-tipping, or from where the rubbish was sourced.
The council said it had also recently issued another £600 fine after a resident's waste was found in a lay-by off Gartree Road in Oadby.
They had not fly-tipped the rubbish themselves, the authority added, but had paid a rogue operator in good faith to take it away.
According to the council, residents have a duty of care for their waste until it is disposed of correctly and should ensure it is given to a licensed waste operator.

Councillor Samina Haq, leader of the council, said: "There is simply no excuse for fly-tipping. It damages our environment, costs money to clear up and is unfair on the overwhelming majority of residents and businesses who dispose of their waste responsibly.
"These successful cases send a clear message that we will investigate reports, gather evidence and take action against those responsible.
"Please continue to report fly-tipping whenever you see it and, if you pay someone to remove your waste, always make sure they are properly licensed."

Health NZ has made hundreds of workers redundant since it was formed in 2022, only to hire at least 166 of them back again.
That's according to documents obtained under the Official Information Act (OIA) by the Public Service Association (PSA).
"Health NZ has identified 166 former employees across the organisation who were made redundant and subsequently returned to work for Health NZ as employees," it said.
The data did not count staff who were made redundant and returned as contractors.

Health NZ (HNZ) said it could not provide data on contractors - generally paid a higher rate than employees - as they were "generally not engaged or paid through Health NZ's payroll systems and are instead recorded through financial systems as vendors".
It said that information would take staff away from their other work for too long to collate.
The 166 staff were from across the organisation and it was not clear what their roles were and whether they were frontline, clinical, or back-office.
Agency-wide, 1907 redundancy payments had been logged in the payroll system since 1 July 2022.
"This figure has been compiled from more than 20 payroll systems and may include both voluntary redundancies and redundancies arising from organisational change."

HNZ could not immediately provide answers on how much had been paid out in redundancies, saying the request would be treated as another OIA, along with questions from RNZ about what exact roles those 166 staff were in, and the amount of time between their dismissal and rehire.

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons said the data revealed "a senseless merry-go-round where health workers lose their jobs creating serious stress to them and their colleagues only to be hired back when Health NZ realised how critical their work was".

"This is exactly why we need a public good test," she said. "Before any major restructure, agencies should have to show what it will do to services and what it will really cost. A public good test would have prevented much of this waste.
"Instead, we've had short-sighted cuts that leave the country less able to cope with an ageing population and growing health needs."
The rehiring data came as part of a request by the union for information regarding data and digital staff in particular.

According to the health agency's employee payroll systems, there were 292 staff members working in a data or digital function who were made redundant since the district health boards (DHBs) were amalgamated to form Health NZ four years ago.

"Employees may be made redundant in one district and rehired in another," it said. "Employees may be made redundant from one role and continue working in another - these employees are excluded from this total."

Robyn Shearer, HNZ's executive national director for people and culture, health and safety, said the agency had combined 20 former district health boards and other health entities when it was established in 2022, and inherited a range of legacy systems, structures and ways of working.
Since then it had undergone "significant organisational change", including the disestablishment of some roles and the creation of new ones.
"We continue to actively recruit to frontline clinical and support roles across Health New Zealand," Shearer said.
Eligibility for redundancy payments was based on the circumstances at the time an employee left Health NZ.

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/regional/2798: After weeks of controversial headlines and hours of public submissions, Wellington's mayor is still holding back from stating his position on the capital's major rating debate.

In an interview with RNZ, Little was asked what his view was on the controversial policy. He said he did not want to pre-empt the process.

"The whole issue of pre-determination does loom large in local government, so we are sensitive to it, particularly on big and controversial questions like this, so it is important we don't look like we've made up our minds before we've made a decision - otherwise people get cynical about the whole consultation process."

Little, however, said feedback from the community , and information received in the consultation process, would "weigh heavily" on the council's decision over its rating system, and suggested it would feature in his.

"I was neutral from the outset, although I'd met with people who were kind of, championing the cause, they could never explain to me what the impact would be, and until I was clear about that I didn't have a view one way or the other, but now I've got some good information to make a decision."

The campaign has involved vocal lobby groups on either side of the debate - Common Ground Aotearoa and Voice for Wellington, including donations for some councillors during the campaign from Common Ground Aotearoa and donations to other councillors from businesses or property developers.
Little said that was the nature of politics in New Zealand, where public funding wasn't provided for those who wanted to stand.
"There wouldn't be a councillor who hasn't had a donation from somebody who represents one view or another."

"I'm not phased by lobby groups, interest groups, pressure groups - whatever. It actually enriches our public debate. I think the job of those in elected public office is to use those discriminatory tools and understand that things said with the greatest passion or volume aren't necessarily correct."
Independent councillor for the Pukehīnau Lambton ward, Nicola Young, said the ratings debate was "boiling over" in the city.
"I've been a councillor for 13 years, and never have I experienced the level of public concern that I have about this.

"I went to the orchestra, people came to me beforehand, during the interval and as I was going home. I'm getting emails all the time, people will stop me in the street - people are worried sick about it."
Hours of back-to-back public hearings held in council offices this week have canvassed a range of views on the different proposals.

A coroner is warning pregnant women that midwifery registration does not guarantee a standard level of experience after the death of a 33-year-old and her baby.
Maria Hune Pirihira Neho died from a catastrophic haemorrhage in 2023 after a uterine rupture during an obstructed labour at her Waikato home.
After an almost three-week inquest, Coroner Ian Telford found the rupture was exceptionally rare and could not reasonably have been predicted or diagnosed beforehand.
But his inquest also highlighted what he said were significant shortcomings in antenatal assessment, birth planning and labour management.

"Including failures to adequately investigate and understand Ms Neho's epilepsy history, shortcomings in decisions regarding the appropriate place of birth, and missed opportunities to recognise abnormal labour at an earlier stage."
Those shortcomings did not cause the uterine rupture, but Telford said they did contribute to a situation where definitive treatment was not immediately available when the emergency happened.
"Hospital-based labour would have provided immediate access to specialist obstetric assessment, theatre facilities, anaesthetic support, blood products, and emergency surgical intervention."
He warned that families considering a community birth should understand how far they are from a hospital and what community practitioners and ambulance staff can do in an emergency.
He said families were entitled to ask a midwife about their experience, support and when she would seek advice or transfer.
Neho had a plan to give birth in the community, at the local birthing centre.
At the time of her death she lived with her partner in Huntly and was the mother of three children.
"By all accounts, family was central to her life," Telford said.

"During her pregnancy she continued to care for those around her, including spending periods in Tokoroa assisting her father when he was unwell. She was excited about the pregnancy and her whānau hoped the baby would be a girl. "
On 2 February 2023, she met her midwife at the birthing centre, but at only 2cm dilated she was sent home to allow the labour to progress further.
About six hours later her midwife was called to their home, because labour had progressed and Neho didn't feel able to travel.
Labour continued, until the midwife said she was fully dilated but the baby was face presenting.
Soon after, when Neho was being prepared to move, she had what was thought to be a seizure.
Attempts were made to stabilise her over the next hour and she was transferred to Waikato Hospital where they did an emergency caesarean, but both mother and baby were declared dead.

While the seizure did not contribute to the rupture or haemorrhage, Telford said experts agreed that Neho's epilepsy history and the uncertainty about recent seizures and treatment meant she should have been strongly advised to give birth in hospital.
She did not give a complete epilepsy history, but did disclose seizures and past medications, and he said these needed further enquiry and a review of records.
Telford said the lead maternity carer showed limited understanding of epilepsy in pregnancy and didn't take reasonable steps to understand the significance of that.
Both midwives who gave evidence at the inquest said they relied almost exclusively on patients' self-reported histories.
One said in her nine years of practice, she had never one accessed a clinical workstation to look at medical records, something that Telford said was alarming.

"Oceania Rugby is cooperating fully and they remain members of World Rugby."

New Caledonia, French Polynesia and Wallis and Futuna operate under the French Rugby Federation.

Oceania Rugby has not responded to RNZ Pacific's questions abut its suspension.

PNG is suspended from Oceania and World Rugby membership, their reinstatement pending systemic and management changes ordered by Oceania Rugby.
Lakapi Samoa was suspended last month following management issues raised by the Samoan government, which has withdrawn support for the national union.
A rival union, the Samoa Rugby Football Union, has since been registered in Apia, with the government's support going towards it.

That happened two weeks after Oceania Rugby had confirmed the tournament was happening in partnership with New Zealand Rugby, Bay of Plenty Rugby and Rotorua Tourism.
While speaking on a possible regional competition to be hosted by Fiji, Sanday said he was hopeful island unions would work with the Oceania body.

"I have urged the few unions that have approached, to work through Oceania as we are all members," he said.

Drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy should come with diet and exercise advice and support say NZ’s peak exercise industry body.
The increased use of weight-loss drugs could put people at risk of bone fractures and increased frailty from unchecked muscle loss, according to New Zealand's peak exercise industry body.
Its Australian counterpart just released new clinical resources for GPs overseeing patients on the medication.
Exercise New Zealand had been speaking to the health minister and the ministry about recommending resistance training and sufficient protein intake to help preserve muscle strength.
GLP-1s like Wegovy are transforming weight loss, but behind the hype, not everyone responds as they hope.
Effective obesity management drugs like Wegovy are framed as "forever" medications. That's a problem when it costs $400 a month.
The weight loss and diabetes drug, which is only available on prescription, should be on pharmacy shelves within days ending a years-long wait for the much-hyped medication.

It wanted this advice to accompany the prescribing of GLP-1-based medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy.
Exercise NZ chief executive Richard Beddie told RNZ’s Nine to Noon Wegovy was a positive drug for people trying to lose weight but had side effects.
The weight loss did not all come from fat loss on the drug and people were really trying to reduce their fat levels rather than their weight, he said.

"We know from meta analyses from many different journals that that loss of fat is around 75 percent at best and sometimes as low as 60 percent, so 25 to 40 percent of that sometimes is lean muscle tissue, in other words muscle, and that has a number of risks with it."
Existing research showed resistance training and sufficient protein was a solution to that, he said.
Clinical trials indicated that it was the same muscle loss that would occur if people lost weight through extreme dieting but weren't on weight loss drugs, he said.
Users did not just need access to information, they needed support, he said.
"Many people will not know how to do resistance training,” he said.

Resistance training - which puts load on the muscles and bones - ensured the body maintained muscle mass, he explained. GLP-1 users should get advice from a professional about the level of training they should be doing.

"It won't stop it [muscle loss] completely, so most of the research says it drops down to sort of between 10 to 15 percent of lean muscle tissue is lost if someone's on GLP-1s for an extended period."
It was harder for people to regain lost muscle mass as they aged, he said.
"For many people if they lose muscle mass, particularly if they're in their 50s or 60s or 70s, they may never get it back."
He said the other focus was around protein because people on weight loss medication didn’t eat much - that’s how the drug worked, he said.

"If someone maintains a poor diet, in other words eating highly processed foods , that's very likely they'll be deficient in protein and when they cut out even more food they're particularly deficient in protein. So the message is around making sure you maintain protein intake as much as possible in the context of you won't be eating much food."
Beddie said information about the importance of resistance training and protein intake should be included as a part of any prescription for GLP-1-based medications.

However, many older Chinese migrants in Auckland are finding that taking some time to learn English helps them gain independence, build confidence and develop a stronger sense of belonging in New Zealand.
According to the latest Census, more than 279,000 individuals in New Zealand identified as Chinese in 2023 , with nearly 70 percent living in Auckland.

The Ministry for Ethnic Communities said people with limited English proficiency could face difficulties accessing health, education, housing and employment, making it harder to settle in New Zealand and live independently.
For older migrants who speak little English, even routine tasks can present significant challenges.
Community English classes have become a place for them to develop the language skills they need to navigate everyday life, from catching a bus to visiting a doctor.
On a rainy Wednesday in Auckland, a group of older Chinese immigrants aged 60 to 85 gathered at the Browns Bay Senior Citizens Club for their weekly English lesson.
The topic of the day was a seemingly simple task: taking the bus to class.
With guidance from their teacher, they practised asking which bus to catch, how long they would have to wait and when they would reach Queen Street.
Seventy-nine-year-old Qingyuan Lu has been learning English with the group for about four years.
He said one of the biggest challenges of learning a new language at his age was his declining memory.
"When I was young, I could remember entire textbooks for exams," he said.
"But now, if I read something in English today, I'll have forgotten it by tomorrow. And it's only getting worse."
Seventy-nine-year-old Qingyuan Lu has been learning English for about four years.
Despite those difficulties, Lu said the weekly classes had become an important part of his life, providing him with a social network and making everyday tasks easier.
"If I can't find a toilet, I can simply ask, 'Where is the toilet?' in English."
"When I'm at the supermarket, I can also manage things like checking out [items] on my own," he added.
For Junrong Liu, 70, six years of English lessons have brought a similar sense of progress.
When she first joined the class, she barely knew the English alphabet.
Junrong Liu, 70, has been learning English for six years and can now confidently talk about her family in English.
Learning English, Liu said, had changed not only her daily life but also the way her family saw her.
"My daughter told me, 'Mummy is very good. Yourself make everything' [sic]."
Bronwyn Young, an English teacher with English Language Partners North Shore in Auckland, has been teaching older Chinese migrants for about 17 years.
Over that time, she has taken pride in watching many of her students progress from barely knowing English to confidently holding conversations with locals.
"I had a student many years ago who said she only spoke to me in English," Young said.
"I had to give her strategies to maybe go for a walk and speak to someone she sees.
"It sort of opened the door for her to speak to everyone, and now her English is quite good."
Young said older students tended to learn more slowly than children and needed more repetition.
She regularly used pictures in her lessons to help students understand and remember new words.
Bronwyn Young has helped older Chinese migrants learn English for about 17 years, watching many progress from knowing only a few words to confidently chatting with locals.
A second-generation Chinese New Zealander herself, Young has also learnt some Mandarin to help her connect with her students and make her lessons easier to follow.

A young man who needs a wheelchair says his rented home set-up prevents his independence and means he requires home help - at a cost to ratepayers.
Flynn Mitchell spends as little time as possible at his Auckland flat, even though he's paid to have ramps installed so he can move between rooms.

He has been part of a sounding board for the Laura Fergusson Trust's bold plans to invest $100 million building 160 highly automated homes for physically disabled people, designed to allow them to live as independently as possible .
Mitchell is 23 years old and has just started a summer internship, but the hardest part of his week is coming home to a flat that doesn't meet his needs.
"Home should be a place where you can rest and chill and at the moment that's my biggest struggle," he said.
"I'm stuck with a place right now that doesn't fit my needs and I come home and instead of chilling it's another battle that I have to put up with and that shouldn't be the case for anyone."
The kitchen and bathroom are pressure points - the toilet is two ramps down from the bathroom.
The toilet in Mitchell's home is two ramps down from the bathroom.

The stove is unusable, the bench in the kitchen too high and the sink too deep for Mitchell to do his own dishes - he gets government assistance for this but would prefer to be able to do the dishes himself.
"I'm essentially doing a pretty half-arsey job on the dishes, it's an old school set up."
Mitchell has Friedreich's ataxia, a neuro-degenerative disorder that since his teenage years has affected his ability to walk.
"I was born a fully normal child, I didn't have any health complications. I actively played football, was running cross country, and took part in sailing," Mitchell said.
"When I was diagnosed, very quickly within the next coming years, I became weaker, was physically uncomfortable in my surroundings. I was off balance, I was weak, very easily hurt."

He gained a Master of Business degree in Entrepreneurship and Innovation from the University of Otago, and for three of his four years in Dunedin, lived in an accessible flat with friends who were not in wheelchairs.
Flynn Mitchell has been part of a sounding board for the Laura Fergusson Trust.

"The flat that I moved into was amazing ... it was all designed for a wheelchair person and to have flatmates as well, they weren't in a wheelchair, which I found awesome because it was me and my mates in a flat," he said.
It was a shock to many when the Laura Fergusson Trust closed its rehab and respite facility in Auckland six years ago, due to years of deficits, but the trust was on the comeback.
Its chief executive Ray Finch said it had $100m funding and the first sites earmarked to start building 160 high-tech accessible homes for physically disabled people, in Auckland.
"The heartache and the conversations with families around people losing their independence or not having their own space are the things that have driven us to this point."
Finch said there were 269 disabled people under the age of 65 living in Auckland's aged care facilities who shouldn't be there.

The Norwegian-Swedish company Wallenius Wilhelmsen has told vehicle importers it will suspend its Japan-to-Oceania roll-on/roll-off service for the year, citing ongoing capacity pressures across the global vehicle shipping market.
The suspension is not expected to impact the import of used hybrid vehicles, or new electric vehicles, or the Nissan Leaf which is imported through a different shipping line.
Vehicle importers say the timing hits as used car prices in Japan are dropping, and demand in New Zealand and Australia is growing.
Greig Epps is the chief executive of the Imported Motor Vehicle Industry Association which represents businesses importing, preparing, wholesaling, and retailing used vehicles.
He told Nine to Noon Teslas, BYDs and BMWs that had been sold into Japan and were now about four or five years old were being brought to New Zealand but perhaps not for much longer.
"We're losing that ability to have some wider choice in the used EV market."
So far this year, about 3500 used EVs have arrived in New Zealand and that might drop to about 2500 next year.
Demand had risen in part due to the Iran conflict , Epps said, and Wallenius Wilhelmsen's decision was a setback.
"This has put a real stop to the used import sector being part of the solution to bringing in reduced emission vehicles."
Used hybrids are more readily available because New Zealand can import them from Japan, an expert says
While the new vehicle market was able to tell producers what brands they wanted, it was much harder to source used EVs in the $15,000 to $20,000 range although hybrids were more readily available.

"What we need to do is look to the hybrids.... When it comes to affordable hybrids we are starting to really hit our straps in the used car space because we can look to Japan which has just focused on hybrids in the last 10 years and we can go back to a vehicle from 2018, 2019 and bring that in and with that we can add to that reduction [in emissions] we're trying to help."
It would also be important to expand the number of new EVs and gradually they would make their way into the used car sector, he said.
China last year produced 34.5 million new vehicles while Japan was next with 8.5m.

"Europe wants it, the US wants it, all these other countries want it and we're at the end of the line and when they come down here, is there anything for them to take away. Empty ships don't make money."
Some importers were looking at containers but with just two EVs per container "it's a lot more expensive".
It was possible shipping companies were nervous of the small risk of the EVs catching fire because the damage would be enormous, given the fires in their batteries were so difficult to put out.
The ships were worth around $150 million and took years to build, so it was understandable if the shipping companies were a bit apprehensive, Epps said.

A representative football player lured a drunk woman out of a pub and took her to a nearby casino where he was seen on CCTV trying to kiss her as she pulled away from him.
Shinnichiro Joey Omotani then helped the woman into a taxi and took her to his home, where he left her sitting on the footpath with her head in her hands for "a lengthy time".
He took a photo of the victim, telling a friend in Australia that she looked "dead".
But instead of calling for help or police, the 28-year-old dragged her into his house and sexually assaulted her twice.
The victim woke once during the night, noticing Omotani beside her, and told him to "f*** off", before passing out again.
Her next memory was walking to the entrance of Lake Rotoroa on Hamilton's Lake Crescent and calling her partner to pick her up.

Omotani, a midfielder, has played for clubs in New Zealand and Australia, including Waitākere United youth (2016), North Shore United (2016-2017), West Coast Rangers, Melville United and Hamilton Wanderers.
He appeared for sentencing in the Hamilton District Court on Wednesday after being found guilty on two charges of sexual violation by unlawful sexual connection.
The circumstances of the case, including the victim's loss of memory, also led Judge Noel Cocurullo to discuss whether her drink had been spiked.
In her victim impact statement, she described waking up in a strange house with no idea where she was, how she got there, or who she was with.
"Having no idea what had happened to me was terrifying, and all I wanted to do was get out of there.
"This was the most traumatising day of my life, and I am still affected by it today."
She had to endure an invasive sexual assault inspection, have photos taken by police of the many bruises on her body, and get treatment for infections she suffered as a result of Omotani's actions.
Compounding the physical and psychological impacts was waiting nearly three years for a jury trial and being cross-examined for "hours and hours was excruciating and humiliating".
She hoped by going through with the trial and speaking out that it might prevent something similar happening to someone else.
The victim had been drinking with friends at an inner-city pub in Hamilton in October 2023.
By 3am, the lights in the pub turned on, and Omotani moved away but remained nearby as the victim spoke with her remaining friends.
As she walked out and was separated from them, Omotani waited as she finished her drink, then quickly grabbed her arm and pulled her out of the bar and walked up Victoria Street.
About 10 minutes later, they arrived at Sky City Casino holding hands.
Omotani continually grabbed her or put his arms around her when she pulled her hand away.
As he withdrew $80 from an ATM, she was approached by two of her friends.
Two minutes later, the pair were denied entry into the casino but instead of leaving, he led her into an elevator.
For about nine minutes, CCTV showed Omotani pulling the victim around the casino carpark, taking her into private corners where they stopped walking and he became "physically very close" to her.
However, his exact actions at those points were unknown because of their distance from the camera.
He then took her back to a lift and continued trying to kiss her as she turned and pulled away from him.
At 3.23am, he pulled her into a taxi outside the casino and went to his house near Hamilton Lake.
During the taxi ride, she sat forward with her head in her hands without saying anything.

The Tauranga District Council has spent more than $7 million on its initial response to the fatal Mauao landslide, expert advice and works to reopen the Bay of Plenty landmark.
And a council report shows while a possible opening date of 20 December has been slated for the summit track, many other features of the tourist attraction will remain closed.
Opening the jewel of Tauranga will depend on getting permission from iwi and the Mauao trust.
Six people died after a landslide at Beachside Holiday Park on 22 January.
The report says workers will need fine weather if they are to complete the work on boardwalks, staircases and walking tracks by 20 December .
And while the summit track could be reopened, it says many of the tracks will remain closed and no timeframe has been provided for them to reopen.
The council has plans to install more fencing on Mauao around closed-off areas and will take six weeks to install security cameras and is looking at requiring people to sign in and out.

Mt Maunganui Ratepayers Association president Michael O'Neill told Morning Report it was "breaking news" that he had spotted in a agenda on Wednesday night.
"This is exciting news and hopefully the council [will] act on it," O'Neill said.
It would be a relief for the business community as well as everyone else in Tauranga, he said.
He agreed January's landslide was a tragedy but said the community's ordeal had "dragged out" for almost a year with the mountain remaining closed.

"It's just about a year now and we keep getting told that the mountain is unsafe. It's always been unsafe it's always had those issues and we've known that for a long time, so to keep telling us that's the reason they're not opening it doesn't actually go down all that well," O'Neill said.
He believed if the council warned people of the risk, they would be covered in the event of any mishap.
Meanwhile, he criticised the announcement that the council's former chief executive was paid more than $150,000 after his resignation.

Following requests under the Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act, the council has revealed a severance payment of almost $131,000 and more than $21,000 towards his legal fees. That's on top of his three-month notice period.
The internal investigation by retired High Court Justice Paul Davison found information identifying a risk to life was received, filed, discussed, forwarded - and then left.
It concluded the landslide was preventable, with "one competent consultant after another" identifying the hazard over two decades.
"Many in the community are pretty unhappy with it. The guy resigned and walked away from the role so why do we have to pay him severance pay and his legal bills," O'Neill said.
The council had said it was meeting his contractual obligations and the $152,000.
More than 500 people had attended a protest meeting on Sunday at council spending and a lack of transparency.
https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/country/27875: South Otago dairy and beef farmer, chartered accountant and shareholder director Will Clarke has been appointed as Farmlands' new chair, having won 87 percent of the vote at this week's AGM.

But the rural co-op's new chair and board has work to do to win over some of its more than 81,000 farmer shareholders, following pushback against its earlier decision to invest in $1 million in AgriZeroNZ over three years.
About 200 people attended the meeting in person, as well as 700 more online. There were 4554 votes cast, from 5.6 percent of all shareholders.

Some shareholders expressed concerns about the lack of consultation and widening scope of the co-op's spending. Others questioned the merit of investing in emissions reductions tools during an over three-hour long meeting in Gore on Tuesday night.

It comes just days after former Farmlands chair Rob Hewett - also the chair of AgriZeroNZ - resigned. A shareholder proposal to remove him was cited as a "significant factor", alongside personal attacks online.

Not all shareholders were opposed to the AgriZeroNZ investment, with one questioning why Farmlands hadn't invested more in methane emissions reductions tools, and another saying shareholders were talking about an investment worth $12 split equally.

However, a resolution asking the board to explore options for exiting Farmlands' existing investment in AgriZeroNZ and to pursue an exit if commercially reasonable passed with almost 60 percent of the vote.
The resolution was non-binding, meaning it was a recommendation to the board and the board will take it under advisement.
Clarke said the board would independently review shareholder communication, processes around the AGM, and consideration of shareholder proposal.
He said the board would report back to shareholders though this would likely take longer than the three-month timeframe put forward in the proposal, as the board's first meeting is in February.

"We intend to take the learnings from this AGM as an opportunity to work more closely with our shareholders to build a stronger future for Farmlands together. We are a co-operative with almost 65 years of history, and we want to ensure we are ready for the next generation. We want to be a trusted partner that our shareholders can rely on."

Another resolution to require shareholder approval by special resolution "for further investments in AgriZeroNZ or related entities, or in other organisations whose dominant purpose is to develop or supply products that reduce methane by altering livestock digestion" received 54 percent percent of the votes, short of the 75 percent threshold required as a special resolution and did not pass.

Laurie Patterson, of Groundswell and a proponent of an earlier resolution to see Hewett removed from the board, withdrawn following his resignation, told those at the AGM he made no allegation of misconduct of improper decision making.
He said it wasn't about Hewett's character but whether the dual chair roles were an appropriate arrangement for the co-op.

Clarke thanked shareholders for "engaging constructively" with the board on their proposals. He was encouraged to see shareholder participation increase to almost 6 percent, "a significant rise from prior years".
He also thanked Hewett for his many years as the board's chair.
"Rob helped guide the co-operative through some difficult years and improve its financial performance."

https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/pacific/27874: Link: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/pacific/2787420%2Fthe-floating-classroom-teaching-kids-to-protect-their-environment

Children on the remote Fijian island of Totoya in the Lau group have been learning from their elders aboard a sailing canoe as part of a programme bringing traditional knowledge back into Pacific Islands classrooms.
The environmental education programme, run by Conservation International, brings teachers and knowledge-holders together to design lessons that reflect their island's culture and environment.

Earlier this month, 45 students from Totoya's four villages took part in a pilot of the programme, weaving food baskets, building a model of their island and sailing on the Uto ni Yalo , a double-hulled voyaging canoe.
Regional project manager Catherina Bolinga said one of the elders on board was the last surviving sailor from Totoya.
"It was really good to see him show the kids and name the parts of the [canoe] while we were on board," she said.
Bolinga said the same elder taught the children to weave baskets, which they then filled with food and carried onto the canoe.
She said elders told her it was the first time they had taught the younger generation to weave, because they usually did the weaving themselves.
Totoya District School head teacher Jone Draunidalo said the pilot has changed how his teachers planned to run their classes.
"Experiential teaching is very important, and we have chosen to use that teaching method," he said.
Draunidalo said lessons can be taken outside the classroom, such as measuring the school playground to learn about area and perimeter, which helps students develop confidence.
"So come next year, we will begin to implement what we have learned from those three days."
School children learning to weave food basket as part of the environmental education programme, run by Conservation International.
Conservation International Fiji director Semisi Meo said the programme is about more than teaching children about nature.
Meo said island communities in Fiji are facing climate change, declining fisheries and the gradual loss of traditional knowledge as people migrate and lifestyles change.
"A society can lose biodiversity and cultural knowledge simultaneously because both rely on the transmission of information across generations."
He said children became noticeably more engaged when lessons were connected to their own island.
"When a community begins teaching itself again, one can reasonably conclude that something important is working."
The programme is modelled on Guardians , a project in Samoa launched in 2018, that used a voyaging canoe as a classroom to teach children about looking after the ocean.
Its founder, Conservation International senior director of marine heritage Schannel van Dijken, said voyaging knowledge was not being taught in Pacific schools.
"These canoes were actually our floating classrooms," he said.
Van Dijken said Pacific ancestors had to understand navigation, plants, food and biodiversity to voyage across the ocean and return.
"You can't teach this intimate understanding of how to live on an island and how to navigate and how to voyage, in a classroom. It needs to be outside. It needs to be experiential."
The Samoan lessons have since been included as supplementary material in the country's primary school curriculum.
The approach is now being adapted for Fiji and the Cook Islands, funded by New Zealand's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade through the Manaaki Fund and by the Global Environment Facility.
Van Dijken said those projects end in the middle of next year, and the focus now is finding new partners.
https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/friends-p: Two best friends have set a Guinness World Record for the highest-ever game of chess played on a mountain, after climbing all the way to the summit of an Ecuadorian volcano to do it.

Americans Adam Wininger, 32, and Joshua Host, 44, set up their chess board at the top of Chimborazo, a mountain in Ecuador, at a height of 20,593 feet, which is more than 6,200 metres above sea level.
Their climb beat the previous record of 20,393 feet, which was set by two British climbers on a mountain in Nepal back in 2024, by exactly 200 feet.
The pair had actually tried to reach the summit once before, but bad weather forced them to turn back. This time, they made it all the way to the top with their chess set in hand.
“It’s our favourite game and there is something so epic about playing it on top of a mountain,” Wininger told Guinness World Records.
He joked that if anyone ever beats their record, the pair will simply climb even higher to reclaim it, by exactly 200 feet every time.
For now, the chess-loving duo can enjoy their spot in the record books, all the way up in the clouds.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/spacecraf: A European spacecraft has sent back the first close-up pictures of an asteroid that was deliberately smashed into by a NASA spacecraft, as part of a test to protect Earth one day.
The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft arrived at the Didymos-Dimorphos asteroid system this week and released its first detailed images on 25 November 2026.

Dimorphos is a small “moonlet” asteroid that orbits a larger asteroid called Didymos. Back in 2022, NASA deliberately crashed a spacecraft called DART into Dimorphos, in the first-ever test of what scientists call “planetary defence.”

The idea is simple: if a dangerous asteroid were ever heading towards Earth, could humans crash something into it to change its path and keep our planet safe? The DART test showed that it can work. The impact changed Dimorphos’s orbit around Didymos by just over 30 minutes.
Now Hera’s job is to study the crater DART left behind, to help scientists understand exactly what happened and how big the effect was.
“ESA’s Hera mission has arrived to learn the answers we need to know,” said mission lead Patrick Michel.
Hera will stay at the asteroid system for months, using cameras and other instruments to learn more about how to keep Earth safe from space rocks in the future.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/christchu: A 25-year-old model and entrepreneur from Christchurch has placed fifth at the 75th Miss Universe pageant, New Zealand’s best result at the competition in more than 40 years.

The crown this year went to Miss Puerto Rico, Jennifer Barreto, with Miss Dominican Republic and Miss Venezuela also making the top five.

Waddington’s result is already being celebrated back home as a proud moment for New Zealand on the world stage.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/giant-new: Northland has its first wind farm, with power company Mercury officially opening the $287 million Kaiwaikawe Wind Farm near Dargaville on Monday.

The wind farm sits at Ōmāmari, on the region’s west coast, on farmland run by Pāmu. Mercury chief executive Stew Hamilton cut the ribbon alongside Kaipara Deputy Mayor Gordon Lambeth and Northland MP Grant McCallum.
“Today we recognise the skill and commitment of everyone who has helped bring Northland’s first wind farm to life,” Hamilton said.

The wind farm has 12 huge turbines, each standing 206 metres tall from the ground to the tip of the blade when it’s pointing straight up. That makes them the tallest turbines in New Zealand, and the second-tallest structures in the whole country, beaten only by Auckland’s Sky Tower.
Together, the turbines can make about 77 megawatts of electricity. That’s enough power for more than 31,000 homes once the wind farm is running at full strength.
Construction began in March last year, and Mercury says the project remains on schedule and on budget, with full power generation expected by 2027.
“We remain on track to complete the Kaiwaikawe development on schedule and on budget,” Hamilton said.
Wind farms like this one help New Zealand make electricity without burning fuels like coal or gas, which is better for the environment and for the climate.

Another section shows maps, ship sketches, and short captions about travel at sea. https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/air-nz-br: Air New Zealand is flying long-haul routes from Christchurch again, after a non-stop flight to Singapore took off on 28 October 2026. Long-haul flights are very long trips, often across oceans. Since 2020, the airline had flown very few of them from Christchurch.
More routes are on the way. Direct flights to Tokyo in Japan start on 28 November, and flights to Perth in Australia start on 30 November. A seasonal service to Bali is planned for winter 2027.

Christchurch Airport is expecting its busiest international summer yet, with 21 percent more international seats than before. That’s roughly one extra seat for every five. Even so, Auckland still handles nearly three times as many passengers.

Will smaller towns benefit? Christchurch is also a hub, or meeting point, for flights to smaller places like Queenstown, Dunedin, Nelson, Hokitika and Invercargill. Ajai Jayathilakan, an aviation lecturer at Massey University, warns that these regional communities could miss out.

Figures from NZ Airports looked at routes where another airline, Jetstar, doesn’t compete with Air NZ. On those routes, fares rose 4.2 percent and seat numbers dropped by the same amount. Billie Moore, who led NZ Airports at the time, said, “Regional New Zealand is living the reality of this every day.”
Jayathilakan says the new flights are good news for the South Island. He says ideas like better-linked flight timetables could help smaller towns share in the benefits.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/famous-ba: One of the Batmobiles from the 1992 film Batman Returns is going up for auction near Los Angeles, in the United States. It could become the most expensive Batmobile ever sold.

Julien’s Auctions expects the car to sell for between US$5 million and US$7 million, which is about NZ$9 million to NZ$12 million. The current record is US$4.6 million (about NZ$8.4 million). It was set in 2013 by the Batmobile Adam West drove in the 1960s Batman TV series.
Three special Batmobiles were built for Batman Returns, which was directed by Tim Burton. Julien’s calls this one the “Number One Hero car”, and it was used in most of the film’s driving scenes.
The glossy black car is about six metres long and has two large tail fins. It still has its original paint, a Chevrolet V-8 engine, and a remote-controlled exhaust that shoots out flames.
Julien’s called it “one of the most recognised and important cinematic vehicles in Hollywood history.”
However, the new owner won’t be cruising the streets in it. The car is not street legal, which means it can’t be driven on public roads. It must also stay parked whenever it’s shown to the public.
The car has spent years on display at the Marconi Automotive Museum in California, and the auction takes place in Gardena on Tuesday.

https://www.kiwikidsnews.co.nz/black-cap: The Black Caps battled through a windy final day at the Basin Reserve in Wellington to draw the first cricket Test against India on 23 November 2026.
India had scored 720 runs for nine wickets before declaring, which means choosing to stop batting. That gave them a huge lead of 352 runs.

To save the match, New Zealand had to bat for the whole day without losing all their wickets. They started at 119 for two and played so carefully that it took 18 balls to score their first run of the morning.

Devon Conway made 65 and Rachin Ravindra made 37 before both were out. Glenn Phillips, who scored a century in the first innings, made 26. He and Daryl Mitchell put on 63 runs together, and Mitchell finished not out on 49.
New Zealand were 239 for five when the captains shook hands to end the match. India were still five wickets short of a win.
In Test cricket, if time runs out before either team can win, the match is a draw.
